One of the milieus that I talk about a lot in the book is Exile Land, which is this network of Russian radical colonies all over Western Europe. Exile Land is not just a place that the Bund retreats to. This is the stomping ground of all the revolutionaries who will shape the future Soviet Union. Kamenev is from Exile Land. Grigory Zinoviev, Trotsky, Lenin — utter Exile Land. Nikolai Bukharin, Karl Radek . . . In the context of the Russian Empire, the machinations of thinkers and leadership who were abroad were as important as the on-the-ground organizing inside the empire, sometimes more important. The Bundists were no exception. Inside the empire, they’re creating labor unions; they are doing self-defense against pogroms. They’re educating shtetls. They’re setting up mutual aid. They’re doing these very practical things. But outside the empire, that’s where they are developing theory. It’s where they are writing these formative texts that will then get smuggled into the empire. It’s where they’re raising money to buy weapons. Sometimes when Jewish groups are talked about, Bundist or Zionist or whatever, there’s this idea that these groups existed in isolation — that there was a Jewish history separate from a Russian history, separate from a European history. But in actuality, these Jewish groups were part of this diasporic, exiled, multiracial, multiethnic, multireligious revolutionary scene, and they were all interwoven. They all slept with each other. They all owed each other money. They all had interminable beefs with each other. They all influenced each other, whether positively or negatively. And the dynamics of these incestuous communities in Western Europe fundamentally shaped how the Russian Revolution would shake out. The Bund’s Jewish Rivals Daniel Denvir The Bund was a powerful pole of Jewish politics, sometimes an extraordinarily powerful pole at certain moments in its history. But it wasn’t the only political and social force engaged in the struggle for political power in the Pale. There were, of course, more Orthodox religious Jews, against whom the Bund was rebelling in many ways. And after 1897, there were Zionists. What was the balance of power between the Bund and these other forces? What did the struggle for political power look like inside the Pale among Jews? And how did the Bund view its Jewish rivals and enemies through the lens of its own socialist ideology? Molly Crabapple Jewish politics — I’m going to say something shocking — has always been pretty disputatious and diverse. In the Pale of Settlement, there were a number of different political actors. There are bourgeois assimilationist Jews who just want to be fancy Russians at the end of the day. There are Jewish Bolsheviks and Mensheviks. There are Jewish Socialist Revolutionaries. There are Jewish anarchists — Bialystok was a major center for Jewish anarchism. There are pious Orthodox Jews who have their own disagreements with each other. Not to go on a tangent, but in addition to the Hasidic Jews, there was another very pious Orthodox sect called the Misnagdim, who were founded to say Hasidic Jews were doing sh-t wrong, and that you shouldn’t be doing ecstatic prayer. You should be doing study. There was a lot of dispute. And there were Zionists. People sometimes imagine that the Zionist movement was a single thing because it was able to act in a cohesive and unified way in the creation of Israel and the Nakba. But the Zionist movement was a divided movement. You had fancy-pants bourgeois Zionists like Theodor Herzl. You also had a movement that was called Labor Zionism, and Labor Zionism is a very interesting and wacky movement that people like to bring up now when they’re trying to make apologia for Zionism, because they’re like, “The Labor Zionists were socialist.” But I want to talk a little bit about what Labor Zionism was. Labor Zionism was led by a guy named Ber Borochov, who was in the same milieu as the Bund. The idea was that Jews were not able to develop into economically normal people, because of their position as a minority in Europe. And what did he mean by “economically normal”? He meant that Jews were not doing big-d-ck, manly man, hammer-swinging jobs, like in steel mills or coal mining. Borochov meant that Jews were just doing effeminate and weak jobs, like tailoring or shoemaking. The idea was that if Jews wanted to become big-d-ck, broad-shouldered, manly hammer swingers, they could not keep existing as a minority in Europe. They had to go to Palestine, and in Palestine, they would set up a Jewish state with Jewish socialists and Jewish workers and Jewish capitalists — Jewish exploiters. And eventually, the Jewish workers would do a revolution against the Jewish exploiters, and there would be communism. This was the great idea that Borochov had. Borochov did not think that there were going to be issues between the Palestinians in Palestine and Jews who were coming in to colonize, because he thought that they were essentially the same, but that Palestinians were kind of lesser. In order to give an example of what a great situation it was going to be in Palestine, he looked at Liberia, where he was like, “Yeah, the African American settlers, they were like brothers to the Kru people they colonized in Liberia. That went great. It’ll be the same in Palestine.” Borochov did not go to Palestine. This was a pamphlet-based view. Now, Labor Zionist groups like Poale Zion were major competitors to the Bund, though they were always less popular. Labor Zionist groups also tried to organize labor unions and to organize resistance against pogroms. But the Bundists were a more powerful faction. In addition to Labor Zionism and the sort of bourgeois, Herzl Zionism, there was also what is called Revisionist Zionism. Revisionist Zionism’s leader was a guy named Ze’ev Jabotinsky. He also came from the same social milieu as the Bund. He, in fact, dated Sofia Dubnova, who would become the wife of the Bund’s leader in Poland. Revisionist Zionists believed in strength. They believed in cruelty. They believed in military conquest of both banks of the River Jordan, and they believed that the cringing, shrinking Jew of the diaspora — Jabotinsky often used the slur “Yid” to describe this Jew — they believed that this cringing, shrinking, effeminate, weak Jew of the diaspora had to be remade into a big, strong, brutish, tall Hebrew, to use Jabotinsky’s words. Talk about self-hating, right? Jabotinsky believed that military discipline and violence and conquest was how you were going to remake the Jewish man. In the Pale of Settlement, Zionism was always more associated with the bourgeoisie. The Bundists always thought the idea of socialist Zionism was inane because they were like, “You call yourself socialists, but you can’t actually live for one day in Palestine without getting infusions of cash from bourgeois Jewish organizations.” Zionism was always intensely dependent on Jewish philanthropy, which like all philanthropy, largely derives from the wealthy. Because of that, it was always in the hock to the elites. Seeing Through Zionism Daniel Denvir The Bund maintained an extraordinarily sharp, very prescient critique of Zionism from the get-go, and it maintained that critique all the way through the Holocaust and then through the foundation of the State of Israel and the Nakba in 1948. It consistently argued that the imposition of a Jewish state on an Arab majority would require a state of perpetual warfare, which turns out to be true. How was it that the Bund’s ideology equipped it to understand Zionism so quickly and so clearly? Molly Crabapple The Bund understood Zionism because it’s actually pretty easy to see through Zionism if you look at what it is and you also consider Palestinians to be equal humans. But I’ll go through the Bund’s critique of Zionism, because they hated Zionists from the start. I have quotes from 1901, where Chaim Weizmann, who’s the future leader of the Sate of Israel, says that everywhere the Zionist’s hardest struggle is conducted against the Jewish Labor Bund. The same year, Bundists are calling Zionists the most evil enemy of the organized Jewish proletariat. This is the level of oil-and-water hatred between these two groups, and there are a number of reasons for that. First, Bundists thought Zionism was wildly impractical. The idea that millions of people would leave their homes and become collective farmers in the Levant was an inanity to them. Second, they hated how, from the very start, Zionist leaders were willing to cut deals with antisemites. There’s a moment in my book where in 1903, the Bundist leader Vladimir Medem goes to one of the World Zionist Congresses as an observer, and on stage, Theodor Herzl brags about setting up a meeting with Vyacheslav von Plehve, who is a notoriously racist minister of the interior that most Jews hold responsible for the Kishinev pogroms. But Herzl doesn’t care. He does not care if the person who he’s trying to cut deals with murdered Jews, because he is purely Machiavellian, and he just cares about colonizing land in Palestine. Third, the Bund also had a philosophical disagreement with Zionists. At a time when so many powers in Europe viewed Jews as swarthy, Oriental, eternal alien others who ought to get out, Zionists agreed. Zionists also thought Jews had no place in Europe. In addition to all of these things, Bundists were able to look logically at the situation and say, if you have a place that is almost entirely Palestinian Arab, and you desire to take over land in that place to make that place majority Jewish, you are going to be in conflict with the people who live there. This is a basic thing that anyone with half a brain cell could realize. If the government of France said that its goal was to acquire even half of New York City and make it so that only French citizens could live there, New Yorkers would be angry at it. No one in the world would like this. No one in the world wants to be kicked out of their homes so that a racially exclusivist entity can be created there. It takes a lot of self-delusion and frankly a lot of white supremacy to not realize this basic fact. The Revolution and the War Daniel Denvir Your book opens up the wide, diverse world of revolutionary organizations operating across the Russian Empire and more broadly across Europe throughout the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, leading up to the Russian Revolution — a signal event for the Bund and for every revolutionary organization in the empire and everywhere. Bundists, you write, always viewed the Bolsheviks as authoritarian and demagogic, from the earliest days of the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party. We talked about how the relationship between the Bund and the Bolsheviks started off bad. How did things get worse leading into 1917? To zoom out, where did the Bund in the months and years leading into the revolution and then through the period of the provisional government fit into the state of competition and conflict with Bolsheviks — and also with Socialist Revolutionaries and Mensheviks and the left and right factions of both of those parties — amid the tumult of the provisional government leading into the Bolshevik Revolution — or, for its detractors, the Bolshevik coup? Molly Crabapple The Bund rejoined the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party in 1907, and it became very close to the Mensheviks. In fact, you have a lot of Bundists who are Mensheviks: Henryk Erlich, Mark Liber. These people would both become prominent Mensheviks and keep their position in the Bund, the way that you have people who are big Jewish Voice for Peace leaders who are also Democratic Socialists of America leaders. The Mensheviks and the Bund were like sister organizations in the same party in the years leading up to World War I. I want to talk for a moment about what World War I meant, not just for the Bund but for Jews in Russia, because it’s really important that listeners understand it in order to understand the position the Bund is in when the revolution breaks out in February. The start of World War I was a calamity for the Jews of the western Russian Empire. The tsarist army considered Jews to be a fifth column, and there were mass deportations from major Jewish cities like Dvinsk. An entire city that was a third Jewish would be emptied out over the course of a few weeks — people shoved into boxcars with what they could carry and dumped out in the interior of Russia and then having their Christian neighbors loot their homes. Jewish life was radically dispersed by these deportations. The Pale of Settlement was destroyed in practice, even though it still had the force of law. In addition to the deportations, there were also massive roundups at the start of the war of all sorts of suspected radicals, but particularly Jewish ones. A number of major Bundist leaders find themselves in Siberian exile. When the war starts, the Russian troops initially have some successes, and they are able to take some land in the Habsburg Empire, where Jews have lived in a state of quasi-equality. Jews in the Habsburg Empire are in a much better position than they are in Russia and largely are extremely loyal Habsburg citizens. When the Russian army sweeps in, they steal these people’s land, they butcher them, they kick them out of their government jobs. It is a disaster that creates mass refugee waves, toward Budapest and toward Vienna, of Habsburg Jews that are fleeing these marauding hordes. Then the German and Habsburg armies start to win, and as the Russian army flees from the collapsing front, it blames all its military losses on the Jews and start doing a series of horrific pogroms as it’s pushed back. In this diary by S. An-sky, a major Jewish playwright who’s doing aid during the war, he talks about how in my great-grandfather’s hometown, the Russian army forced men to strip naked and ride pigs, and then shot a bunch of people, just because. The Pale of Settlement becomes an incredibly bloody front line. Then as the war progresses, Germany and Austria take more land, and major Jewish cities like Warsaw, Łódź, Vilna, and Lublin fall behind enemy lines. The German Army advances farther and farther east, and the areas that they take are the areas of the Pale of Settlement. So by 1917, a vast percentage of Russia’s Jews are now cut off from Russia. They are under German and Austrian occupation and, frankly, in a much better position than they were before, because for all of Germany and Austria’s problems, they were a hell of a lot better than the tsarist empire. Major Bundist leader Vladimir Medem, for instance, is liberated from a czarist jail in Warsaw by the advance of the German Army. In the areas that are controlled by the Germans, the Bund is allowed to more or less freely operate. It’s allowed to set up soup kitchens. It’s allowed to set up communal organizations, labor unions. Sometimes it is repressed, but in general, not so much. From the time that these western provinces fall under German occupation, the trajectory of the Bundists there goes an entirely different way than that of the Bundists in Russia. Now, I want to mention something else, which is that St Petersburg — Petrograd, Russia’s capital, which has now been renamed to sound less Russian — is not a Jewish center, and neither is Moscow. These are places the vast majority of Jews were banned from living in. So, the Bund in these places is essentially a debate society of well-off professionals. It’s a reading group. The Bundists there are largely acting more as Mensheviks than as Bundists. In my book, I follow Henryk Erlich, who’s a Bundist leader, a labor lawyer, a radical. He’s married to my favorite character, the avant-garde poet and revolutionary Sofia Dubnova. But in terms of what he’s doing in Petrograd in the years leading up to the Russian Revolution, he’s essentially a Menshevik political operator, which is not a contradiction. The Mensheviks and the Bund and the Bolsheviks at this point are all in the same party. The Russian Revolution, the first Russian Revolution of March, is not a revolution that is led by any revolutionary party. It is a revolution that starts on International Women’s Day, 1917, when the working women of Petrograd decide that they are done at having their men murdered in a stupid meat-grinder war, and that they are done with the famine, and within a few days, that they are done with the tsar that is causing all of it. The revolution that breaks out is a people’s revolution that owes nothing to any party. It is born of the streets. It is born of poor and working people who attack the troops, who call on each other to overthrow the government that’s oppressing them, and it is also born from the young men conscripted into the tsarist army who do not want to die in a stupid meat-grinder war and who do not want to shoot up crowds of women who look like their mothers. Within a few days of these massive street protests breaking out in Petrograd, revolutionaries march to the only democratic body that exists in the entire tsarist empire, and that is the Duma, this impotent, powerless, not particularly democratically elected but kind of democratic body headquartered in Tauride Palace. It’s at this moment, when these masses of impoverished women, factory workers, and military deserters converge on Tauride Palace to demand leadership from the Duma, that a young, charismatic, extremely vain socialist lawyer named Alexander Kerensky makes his first appearance in history. Unlike all of the other bourgeois, vacillating stuffed shirts in the Duma, Kerensky realizes that this is a moment that these previously powerless parliamentarians can now seize the revolution themselves and they can take leadership of it, and Kerensky goes out to greet the masses as heroes. Within about a day, Kerensky and other more or less progressive representatives of the Duma band together, and they create what’s called the Provisional Government, which will be considered by foreign countries and officialdom as the official government of revolutionary Russia. But another force is also being created. While one group of protesters is converging on Tauride Palace, another group of protesters is going to Peter and Paul Fortress. The protesters converge on Peter and Paul Fortress, where a bunch of political troublemakers, dissidents, leftists, and socialists are locked up, including some guys who have been involved in creating a coordinating council that was particularly important during the previous revolution in 1905. It was called a soviet. These socialists also hurry to Tauride Palace. Among them is a Bundist named Henryk Erlich. Together these socialists form a coordinating committee and send out delegates to all of the factories and army garrisons to ask for representatives, and all of those people together will create a new soviet, the Petrograd Soviet, which is the actual democratic street-level power of the revolution. Imagine the scene: On the right side of Tauride Palace is the official democratic body, the provisional government, and on the left wing of Tauride Palace is the actual chaotic street-level, grassroots, cacophonous democracy of workers and especially soldiers. These two bodies, the official one, the provisional government, and the unofficial power, the soviet, will be the twin poles that come together to try to guide the revolution in its early months and that will eventually pull the revolution apart. Bundists were involved with the Petrograd Soviet from the very start. It was created in part by Erlich. Mark Liber, another prominent Bundist, took a prominent position as soon as he was able to escape from Siberian exile. In the early months of the revolution, it is a sort of ecstasy for the Bund. First, all laws that discriminate against people based on nationality, religion, or aristocratic rank are rescinded. The Pale of Settlement is destroyed forever. The restrictions on education fall. Jews are allowed to participate in government. The New York Times is reporting with astonishment that a Jewish guy named Mr Epstein is now the police chief of Minsk. For the first time, Jews are equal citizens. The Bund becomes a legal organization. It takes over an office in Nevsky Prospekt, the fanciest avenue in Petrograd. It marches with its Yiddish flags as an equal party. It hosts its first legal events. There are these very touching moments that I found describing the Bund’s first legal event in Petrograd, where there’s all these old people there, people who were deep friends who’ve been kept apart by years in prison and exile. They have gray hair now. They’re frail. They’re looking around and they’re like, “Who are all these new kids who joined the party?” They’re trying to pretend that they’re still young themselves, as if all of these years haven’t passed, and they’re in complete wonder. Also, the Bundist Mark Liber becomes the most charismatic and beloved speaker at Tsinsarli’s Circus, the main speaking joint in the city, someone who’s carried off by Kronstadt sailors on their shoulders. The whole city seems like a noisy, glorious, revolutionary cacophony. But there is a problem, and that problem is that Russia continues to be involved in World War I. When Russia was the tsarist empire, the Bund obviously opposed the war. But once the revolution happened, things started to look a little bit different. This is the moment that I find the most vexatious, baffling, maddening, and idiotic in all of the Bund’s history. The Bund decides, through a combination of huffing too much dogmatic Marxist theory and wanting to be seen as respectable by other democratic countries, that it really has to stay in World War I. I remember reading the minutes of this Bundist conference where Liber is making this passionate speech about how Russia can’t betray its commitments to democratic England and democratic France and can’t abandon poor Serbia and noble Belgium. And I feel like I’m watching every single time in my own lifetime when I’ve seen a progressive candidate I got behind defend the indefensible, because defending the indefensible seemed like what a reasonable adult ought to do. For the first weeks of revolutionary ecstasy, the Bund continues its crowded schedule of conferences, of planning, of giving idiotic speeches in support of World War I, until their old enemy from exile land, Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, rolls into Finland Station on April 16, 1917, gets out of his train car, steps onto the back of an armored truck, and delivers a speech that excoriates every single revolutionary in Russia for their idiocy and their weakness. And he’s right. Lenin quickly asserts his control over the Bolsheviks like he always asserted his control over everything, and he hammers home the simple message of peace, land, and bread. Unlike every other revolutionary party and most other revolutionaries, Lenin is able to see the simple truth that the revolution was caused by World War I, and that soldiers who are lynching their officers, soldiers who are told to take their boots off the corpses of their friends, are not going to continue doing that just because the government changed its name. Lenin knows that the only way for the revolution to survive is to end World War I. When I read Bundist accounts of the months up until the October Revolution, there’s a sense of doom. There are these memoirs by Raphael Abramovitch, a Bundist leader who was part of the much smaller antiwar faction, the Bundist Internationalists — he was also a Menshevik Internationalist. The moment he gets back into Russia from exile, all he does is try to persuade the Mensheviks: “Guys, we have to stop being in World War I. If we don’t leave the war, if Russia doesn’t make a separate peace, Lenin is going to take over. We have to make a separate peace. We have to do it while we still have the power.” There’s this scene that I didn’t put in my book, because I had to cut some things, that was just tearing out my heart. Raphael Abramovitch finally gets an audience with a bunch of these pro-war Mensheviks and pro-war Bundists who are on the soviet, and he gives this speech where he says, “The soldiers are lynching their officers and running away from the front. They overthrew the tsar because he got them into this war, and if you don’t get them out of it, they’re going to overthrow you too. You have to get us out of the war while you still have power.” And he looks out at the audience, and everyone is just looking at him with blank hostility. He’s desperate, and he stands on stage and says, “Okay, maybe you have a better plan. Tell me, what’s your plan to save the great Russian Revolution?“ And the chairman of the Soviet sort of mutters something about how that’s a big question and they’ll get to it later, and Abramovitch goes off the stage. Afterward, a bunch of his comrades come up to him privately and say, “You’re totally right.” Abramovitch is horrified, and he’s like, “Why didn’t you back me up then, if I was right?” And they tell him that it would just be too emotionally difficult for them to go against the Marxist theory of historical development that they think obliged them to support a pro-war government. Really, what they mean, in my view, is that they’re too afraid to go against the opinions of their friends. The Circle of Kosher Socialists Daniel Denvir You suggest that the Bund was prescient about the authoritarian form the Soviet Union ultimately took — that the outlines of what happened under Joseph Stalin were visible under Lenin, though you do not conflate the two. What, in your view, did the Bund understand about the Bolsheviks? What, if anything, do you think the Bolsheviks had right about the Bund? Molly Crabapple The truth is, the Bolsheviks were authoritarian from the start. This was a faction that was setting up concentration camps by 1919. They were shooting fellow socialists and padlocking soviets from the very earliest days. They were shooting up workers’ protests. You could argue, maybe they needed that authoritarianism because the world-historical role they were playing was such that they had to suppress other leftist groups who would have prevented them from doing that, yada yada. . . . There is no read of Lenin and of the Soviet Union from its very earliest days that does not acknowledge that they were an authoritarian movement quite comfortable with killing people, including their fellow leftists. That’s just the case. Read Victor Serge about 1918. Anything besides that is fantasy, in my opinion. The Bundists knew the leading Bolsheviks very well. These were people they had spent over a decade living next to in very close proximity. They knew Lenin’s intolerance for dissent. There’s another interesting relationship between Bundists and Bolsheviks, which is Felix Dzerzhinsky, who would become the first head of the Cheka, the Soviet secret police. He was very close to Bundists when he was young. His fiancée, Julia Goldman, the love of his life, who died in his arms of tuberculosis, was the sister of Mark Liber, a right-wing Bundist leader. He shared a jail cell with Vladimir Medem, who was friends with Liber. He was someone who knew Bundists very well, and Bundists also knew how much the horrific torture he had undergone in tsarist jails had changed him. This is a man who nearly had to have his legs amputated because the wounds from his shackles got infected. His jaw was permanently broken askew from being beaten so much. These things change someone. This sort of trauma and abuse changes someone, and the Bund knew that because it knew him very well. So I think that there was an element of personal knowledge that the Bundists had of leading Bolsheviks that influenced how they saw people. But you also have to remember that immediately after the revolution, the Bolsheviks were just really repressive. Bolshevik Red Guards shot up protests in support of the Constituent Assembly, which was in January 1918. This was the most cherished organ of revolutionary democracy historically. This was what everything was supposed to be leading toward, but because the Bolsheviks didn’t win the majority of delegates on the Constituent Assembly, they shot up pro-assembly protests, killed people, and padlocked the building. When workers protested for the eight-hour day that was promised to them, these workers’ protests were shot up. In the very earliest days of Soviet rule in Russia, Bundists are repeatedly arrested and threatened with death. Sometimes they have to go on hunger strike to get out of jail. Outside of the centers of St Petersburg and Moscow, in more Jewish cities in the Pale like Smolensk — cities that used to have a lot of Bundists on the soviets — any time Bundists and Mensheviks won majorities of the soviets, those soviets were padlocked. They were shut down. Bundists were executed or sent to concentration camps or simply disappeared. Bundist funerals were shelled. It didn’t take a genius to see that this was repressive. There’s this great essay by Vladimir Medem, who was in Poland this whole time; he was not in the Soviet Union. He wrote this in 1918, when Trotsky was perhaps the second-most-popular man in the Soviet Union. Medem wrote, “Every day, the circle of kosher socialists grows smaller and smaller. Today Lenin wants to shoot Raphael Abramovitch. Who’s to say that tomorrow he won’t want to shoot Trotsky?” And while Lenin never wanted to shoot Trotsky, the state that he built sure did. I think that came from the basic insight that if you start your revolutionary project by murdering other socialists, soon you’re going to be murdering each other. I’m sure tankies have a very good reason that they did all that stuff, but for me, my opinions are clear. The Golden Age in Poland Daniel Denvir In the years between the October Revolution and the Nazi occupation of Eastern Europe, the Bund took on a new life within its homeland, within Poland itself, within the former Pale. How would you characterize this chapter of the Bund? What sort of world were they able to create in both small shtetls and big cities like Warsaw? And what did their politics look like? Molly Crabapple By 1923, the Bund no longer existed in the Soviet Union. Bundists either were forced to liquidate their party and join the Communists, or else they were repressed, arrested, and killed. But over the border in Poland, which was now an independent country, the Bund would reach its peak. In independent Poland, the Bund, for the first time in its history, had a place where it could openly build, and it built magnificently. It created an entire alternate world of beauty and of hope for the impoverished Polish Jewish working class. It created Boy and Girl Scouts, a teen movement called Tsukunft, a women’s movement that fought for equal pay and for childcare. It had summer camps. It held hikes. It created the most popular sports club in the country, Morgenstern. It taught a generation of Jewish kids how to ice-skate and how to swim. It had a sports paper, Worker Athlete , that would cover the friendly games between the Bund’s soccer teams, and it sent athletes to Red Vienna to participate in the Workers’ Olympiad. It created the Medem Sanatorium, a sanatorium for slum kids who were at risk of tuberculosis — but it was so much more than that. They called it “the Children’s Paradise.” It was created by a pedagogue named Shlomo Gilinsky on principles he derived from reading [Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s] Émile . But sometimes when I read about it, it seems like a Montessori school today. At a time when a Jewish kid in Poland would have lived under real violence, when he might have started working when he was ten years old in a factory, when he could expect to be beaten at school, at home, or by a cop who was having a bad day, this was a place where they didn’t hit kids or even punish them. The school believed the children needed to laugh. It allowed kids to create their own kids’ parliament and newspaper, and to make decisions in governing the place. It had scientific museums. It taught these slum kids how to raise rabbits and tortoises and how to eat cauliflower and brush their teeth. It organized entire neighborhoods, and when the men they organized started acting snotty to their wives, the Bundists organized those wives too and told the men to have some feminist principles, as socialists should. The avant-garde poet and Bundist revolutionary Sofia Dubnova became their sex columnist in interwar Poland, where she spoke about the ethics of romance and about women’s right to orgasm. They had extraordinary success in labor unions. They didn’t just organize standard industries but also heavily mobbed-up ones. Bernard Goldstein, their Warsaw enforcer, talks about organizing teamsters and back porters, as they were called — guys who strapped giant wicker baskets to their backs and hauled huge loads of goods through streets that wheeled vehicles couldn’t get through. The Bund organized them. It protected small Jewish traders from the Mafia. It fought against evictions. It ran people for city council, and they won. It also ran people for Jewish communal councils, which was counterintuitive because Bundist leaders were atheists. You have Bundist leaders like Henryk Ehrlich running for Jewish communal councils while saying they oppose circumcision. Bundists had amazing newspapers, both in Yiddish and in Polish. Their Yiddish newspaper didn’t just write about local affairs or Marxist propaganda. They reported about the Scottsboro Boys, about socialists in China, and about the Italian invasion of Ethiopia, and they translated avant-garde literature into Yiddish. Bundists were deeply involved in the championship of Yiddish literature. There were Bundist poets like the great Mordechai Gebirtig, who created songs and poetry that rang out across all of Poland. The Bund defended all this because Poland between the wars was a really racist place. Polish nationalism had this very insecure, paranoid, and insane character that I partially credit to the fact that Poles were only a bare majority of independent Poland. Independent Poland had tons of Ukrainians, tons of Germans; it was about 13 percent Jewish. Cities like Warsaw were a third Jewish. So, a lot of the major political forces in the country were deeply racist. The father of modern Poland, Józef Piłsudski, was an authoritarian nationalist, but he was not racist whatsoever. He was someone who had a multiethnic vision of Poland based on the old Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. He was also someone who knew Bundists very well. He had been intellectual sparring partners with Bundist leaders like Arkady Kremer, and he came up from the world of the Polish Socialist Party, even though he broke with them by World War I. But another major force in Poland was a party called the National Democrats, or the Endeks for short, and this was a Catholic, anti-socialist, anti-leftist, and genocidally racist political party led by one of these masturbatory pamphleteers of the nineteenth century, a guy named Roman Dmowski. You can just imagine these guys crouched over in their dark little dens, pounding out these pamphlets of torrid race science and revanchist border-war fantasy. That’s Dmowski. The Endeks’ vision of Poland was one that was ethnically pure and Catholic, and from the very start they wanted to deport their entire Jewish population and steal all the stuff they left behind. That was their politics. To give you an idea of how crazy the Endeks were, in 1922, Poland has its first-ever election for president, and a liberal guy named Gabriel Narutowicz, a friend of Pilsudski, wins. A lot of minorities vote for Narutowicz, including a lot of Polish Jews. This sends the Endeks into a fury. How dare these Jews exercise their political franchise? They immediately nickname Gabriel Narutowicz “the president of the Jews,” go on days and days of riots, and finally, when Narutowicz shows up at an art exhibit to try to prove that things are normal, an Endek shoots him in the head and kills him, and that guy is celebrated as a hero in the Endek press. This is the level we’re dealing with: a party that murders the first democratically elected president of Poland because Jews voted for him. So from the very start, the Bund needs to physically defend itself, and to this end they turn to a scar-faced bruiser named Bernard Goldstein — my major crush of the book, by the way, which should be obvious to everyone. He creates what’s called the Warsaw Self-Defense Militia. I want someone who has experience with being in the military, being in some sort of armed force, to write about the Warsaw Self-Defense Militia, because I think that a lot of things Bernard says about violence are very interesting. The first thing is that he does not allow anyone except top leadership to have guns, because even though he wants to defend his community, he doesn’t want to leave a trail of murdered people. He wants to teach lessons, which he feels he’s able to do with brass knuckles and spring-loaded steel bats. He is also very concerned with the idea that members of the militia should get special privileges. He really doesn’t want them to be more glorified than other people. He thinks there’s a lot of danger in having a group of armed men who get all of the special privileges and adulation. He thinks there’s the seed of corruption and authoritarianism in there, and so he fights against any sort of special treatment for the militia. Thuggishness, corruption — but also he just doesn’t think that doing violence is more important than other types of work. There’s this part in the book that’s so touching to me, where Bernard goes to the home of his best friend, a Bundist teacher named Shlomo Mendelssohn, whom he really worships. Mendelssohn is erudite; he’s witty. He’s a very good writer. He’s married to a stage actress. He’s an intellectual. Bernard always goes to his house after he’s been in a street fight. And one day, he has this outburst where he says, “I wish I didn’t have to be this guy. I wish I didn’t have to be an enforcer. Why am I always the one who has to stick a gun to someone’s head or break his knees?” He says that he wishes he could have had a life where he sat behind a desk and wrote things, like Shlomo Mendelssohn does. And Mendelssohn, like so many intellectuals, has a crush on thugs, and he says, “Now, Bernard, I wish I was tough like you. I wish I could be you.” Each man kind of wishes they were in the other one’s place, but I think it says something really noble about Bernard that he does not think that doing violence is some elite, cool thing. He thinks of it as a tragic necessity. Daniel Denvir And just happens to be good at it. Molly Crabapple He happens to be good at it — a lifelong enforcer. He defends his community from the mob, from the predations of landlords. One of their techniques is that if a worker’s being evicted, a bunch of these thuggish Self-Defense Group members show up, and they take all the furniture that the landlord threw on the street, and they haul it right back up the stairs and put it in the apartment, and they stand around until the landlord gets the message. He also protects his community from Communists, because one of the brilliant ideas — there are so many brilliant ideas the Soviet Union has, and one of the particularly brilliant ones — is this idea called “social fascism.” What social fascism means, according to the Comintern, is that the real enemy of Communist parties is not the actual fascist party that is in power in Italy at that time; it’s actually the social democratic parties who are distracting workers and keeping them from doing the glorious revolution, yada yada. I think anyone who spends too much time on leftist Twitter should be very familiar with this line of thinking. What this leads to in Poland is a situation that would be extremely funny if there weren’t so many victims of it, where Jewish Communists are shooting and bludgeoning Jewish socialists for control over matzah bakeries’ unions, or for control over the union of a tiny shop making second-rate women’s shoes on Krochmalna Street. There are communists murdering Bundists over control of the most insignificant and penny-ante industries that anyone has ever been in, because the doctrines of Moscow say that this is the most important battle you could be having at the time. So Bernard is constantly involved in brawls and sometimes even in gunfights with Communists. Red Vienna Was the Mecca Daniel Denvir One of the most striking passages in your book describes the Bund’s participation in, or visits to, Red Vienna, the socialist city at the height of its interwar glory. Culturally, the Bund was obviously distinct from the Austro-Marxists. Molly Crabapple Though inspired by them. The whole national cultural autonomy thing was directly inspired by Karl Renner and Otto Bauer. Daniel Denvir What was the meaning of Red Vienna as a place, and as a place in a moment, and what was the significance of that place and moment for the Bund? How did the Austro-Marxists influence and interact with the Bund? Molly Crabapple The idea of national cultural autonomy was something that was originally developed by Austro-Marxists Otto Bauer and Karl Renner, though ironically, they did not see it as applicable to Jews. It was more for dealing with the fact that they were also citizens of the incredibly diverse, multilingual, polyglottal Habsburg Empire, and they were trying to think of a way that all of these very different groups of people could live together. The Bund was directly inspired by that, even though they applied Austro-Marxism to Yiddish-speaking Jews, whom the original Austro-Marxists did not see as a separate group. So theoretically, they were super influenced by them. In terms of Red Vienna — and we’re skipping ahead a little bit in time, because the Bund visited Red Vienna at the end of the 1920s and also in ’31, when they were sending delegations of athletes to the Workers’ Olympiad — Red Vienna was the realization of everything they dreamed of. This city was run according to socialist principles, it was creating beautiful, airy, avant-garde housing estates, it was committed to roses as well as bread, it was sending baby baskets to workers but also creating swimming pools and concert houses — a city where Jews were completely integrated into the government. Like Julius Deutsch, who was Jewish — he was the creator of the Schutzbund, Red Vienna’s self-defense militia. Also, Austria is so much richer than interwar Poland. There’s a really comical part where Bernard Goldstein, the leader of the Warsaw Self-Defense Militia, is visiting Red Vienna in 1931 as part of the Workers’ Olympiad, a socialist alternative to the bourgeois Olympics. So he’s visiting Red Vienna, and as an honored guest, he’s put up at the home of a railway worker. When he sees it, he thinks this guy must be a top lawyer or something, because in Poland only an extremely rich person would live in a house that nice. But in Vienna, that’s where the working class lives. And Bernard is just overwhelmed by the city. He talks about all of these kids in the socialist scouting movement, the Red Falcons, calling “ Freundschaft ! ” to him. Freundschaft means friendship; it’s their greeting. He talks about the vast array of entertainments there, which aren’t just the massive rhythmic-gymnastics pageants telling the story of the triumph of the working class. They’re also bike races and chess tournaments. The whole city is taken over; it’s like a carnival. He talks about the red flags that are everywhere. He talks about the moment when the Bund takes its place in this march that all of the national delegations of athletes do down the Ringstrasse, and the Bund is raising its red Yiddish banner, and they’re like equals in the family of nations. Red Vienna is their shining star. That is what they want to achieve in Poland. And when Bundists go to Red Vienna, they’re going to Mecca. Why Bundists Went Over to the Red Army Daniel Denvir We discussed the immediate Soviet repression of the Bund. It was banned along with other non-Bolshevik parties at the outset of the Russian Civil War. But there were some zigs and zags with Soviet policy during the genocidal Nazi invasion of Eastern Europe. The Soviets would, for a time, release and sort of rehabilitate certain Bundist leaders, and then Stalin would go on to crack down on and murder Bundists again later. But I want to ask about the afterlives of specifically Jewish socialism and communism in the Soviet Union, and the Bund’s influence on all of that. At one time, Bundists went on to staff the ethnic Jewish, or Yiddish-language, section of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, the Yevsektsiya. Others in Poland went into the Kombund, the Communist Jewish alternative to the Bund. In some ways, these groups did cultural and political organizing that echoed the Bund’s work, but integrated — whether willingly or not — into a multinational Bolshevik party. What do you make of these experiments? Was it merely co-optation, or did they in some ways represent the migration of a Bundist logic, a Bundist ideological and organizational DNA, into a new Soviet form? Molly Crabapple It’s important to talk about why those Bundists ended up joining the Communist Party, and that starts by talking about what happened in Ukraine during the Russian Civil War. Apologies to Ukrainian historians — I’m going to give a very simplified view. After the working women of Petrograd kick out the tsar, and socialists in Petrograd set up the Petrograd Soviet, socialists in Kyiv do something similar, and they set up what’s called the Rada , which means council, like soviet, but which quickly becomes a sort of quasi-parliament. These socialists, who are cosmopolitan, humane, liberal men who envision a multiethnic society, also want Ukrainian independence, and they spend the months of Russia’s democratic revolution trying to get it and being marginalized and talked down to by a bunch of Russians who, for all of their liberalism and socialism, definitely think of themselves as superior to Ukrainians and think that Ukraine is their possession and are not willing to give Ukraine autonomy, let alone any sort of independence. So when Red Guards shoot up the pro–Constituent Assembly protesters, this sends shock waves through the Rada in Kyiv, and the leaders decide, “F-ck this. If this is how they’re going to treat the great organ of revolutionary democracy, we are leaving. We want independence now.” And they declare independence. Bundists do not support independence for Ukraine, for a variety of reasons too complicated to get into here, but they are willing to take part in the independent Ukrainian government. The Bundist Moisei Rafes is on the Rada. The Bundist David Lipetz is mayor of Berdychiv. And in the first months of independent Ukraine, it really seems like a place the Bund can work. Yiddish is even declared an official language of Ukraine. There are these gorgeous banknotes produced in Ukraine that have writing in all of the official languages of Ukraine, including Yiddish. There’s Yiddish on the signage. There’s Jewish cultural organizing. There’s a great Jewish thing called the Kultur-Lige. But almost immediately, the humanistic, democratically minded, cosmopolitan intellectuals who run the Rada find independent Ukraine collapsing into a killing field, as it’s faced with an invasion by Soviet Russia and with the aftermath of the deal the Rada cuts with Germany to kick out the Soviet Union. Basically, Ukraine becomes the site of wars of everyone against everyone. The armed forces that are available to the Ukrainian government are barely under their control and are loyal to a Cossack-inspired journalist named Symon Petliura, but even only barely there. These armed forces carry out horrific pogroms. I’m talking one-thousand-people-murdered-in-a-day-type pogroms against Jews. In the years between 1918 and 1921, up to 200,000 Jews are murdered in Ukraine in pogroms that are done by almost every group that is there. The only groups that are vocally against murdering Jews in Ukraine are the anarchist armies of Nestor Makhno and the Red Army. Even the Red Army does pogroms sometimes anyway, but the Soviet Union is officially an anti-racist country, and also Trotsky is leading the Red Army. It realizes that antisemitism is a very potent tool of the White Army, and it comes out very strongly against it. People who are accused of pogrom incitement are subject to the death penalty by the Red Army. Lenin is producing wax-cylinder recordings that are being distributed to all the frontline soldiers, saying, “Don’t do pogroms, guys. I know you want to; don’t. Bad idea.” The Red Army is the most powerful force that is against pogroms, even if Red Army groups sometimes do them anyway. What does this mean for the Bundists who are participating in the ostensible government, the Rada? I’m going to give an example of what happens to David Lipetz, the mayor of Berdychiv. A pretty tough guy; he’s organized self-defense groups before. But a pogromist mob invades Berdychiv, kills a bunch of people, breaks into his home, and mock-executes him and his family, and he’s forced to pay a bribe to save his life — the same sort of thing that an old-timey shtetl Jew would have had to do. He and his comrade in the Bund, Moisei Rafes, and a delegation of other Jewish socialists go to Kyiv, and they say, “Guys, you have to protect us against pogroms. We are your citizens. We are your government officials. You have to protect us.” The Rada says, “Yeah, sure. Totally, we will.” Then there’s another pogrom, also by forces allegedly tied to the government. After that, David Lipetz quits his job as mayor, goes to Kyiv, and enlists in the Red Army under the name David Petrovsky. He will become a general in the Red Army, and after the war he will create the entire military education system of the Soviet Union. That same choice that David Lipetz makes is made by the majority of Bundists in Ukraine, and the reason is because they have no one else but the Red Army to protect them from genocidal pogroms. It’s very much a matter of survival. And there are other reasons. There’s the desire to take part in the first socialist state, regardless of its faults. There’s the desire to live in the place that you’re from and continue living there without repression. But the real thing that makes Bundists go over to the Red Army is the fact that everyone else wants to kill all the Jews. That is what leads to the creation of the Kombund in Kyiv by Moishe Rafes. It’s what leads to the majority of Bundists who are in, Minsk in Belarus, but also in Ukraine, to decide that the party needs to officially ally with the Bund, and it’s what leads them eventually to dissolve the Bund and to join the Communist Party. A number of important, powerful Bundists became leading members in the Jewish section of the Communist Party — most famously Esther Frumkin, who was a passionate advocate of Yiddish and a very forceful person. And all of these people would end up dead in the purges of the 1930s on allegations of Bundism, even though they had rejected it, and even though they had persecuted their former comrades. “Poland Is Our Homeland” Daniel Denvir Let’s turn to the Holocaust. How did the Bund understand what was happening to them as it was happening? Something that was particularly poignant, heartbreaking, and remarkable reading your book is how Bundists held so tightly to their universalist ideology, and the particular insistence that the Polish working class were their brothers and sisters, even as they were being murdered. Molly Crabapple The Bund were committed anti-fascists who had recognized fascism for what it was from the days of Benito Mussolini. It had sent people to fight in Spain to defend the Republic against Francisco Franco’s fascists. It had reported on the conditions in Nazi Germany, and former Bundist labor leaders in America had rescued “Aryan” labor leaders from Germany, Italy, and Austria. The Bund had an analysis of fascism that saw it as not just a threat to Jews but as a threat to the entire world, and particularly to the entire organized working class. At the start of the Nazi occupation, the Bundists clung to that analysis that we are all victims of fascism. I’m going to read a passage that I found interesting for what it shows about their analysis of this. When the librarian Herman Kruk fled the Nazi advance to Vilna, he camped in Vilna, which was not occupied by either the Nazis or the Soviets yet and was surrounded by every sort of refugee, Jewish and not Jewish — so crowded that just the idea of having a piece of floor big enough to lie on was almost an impossible dream. Even in this cheek-and-jowl refugee situation, Bundists were arguing with Zionists, and they were saying, “We’re not just Jews fleeing the Nazi advance. We’re political refugees, like our brothers in the Polish Socialist Party.” And there’s a declaration they publish in 1939: “Poland is our homeland, where we are entitled to equal citizenship rights, where our future lies, and any other solutions offered by Zionists or other Jewish groups are wrong and utopian, as they have always been.” That’s the commitment to seeing themselves as socialists and antifascists who are part of a socialist and antifascist movement. However, the Nazi occupation quickly divides Poland into a caste system. At the top are what are called the Volksdeutsche: these are Polish citizens of German origin who are given all sorts of privileges and basically given the option to be part of the German Übermenschen themselves. Then there are the Poles. Poland was, I would say, the country most persecuted by the Nazis. It was one of the only countries in Europe without a auisling government, without a Waffen-SS. Such Polish collaborators as there were amounted to a police force called the Blue Police, but it was not a country where you had elite-level collaboration like in France, for instance. That was because the Poles were viewed as subhuman by the Nazis. The Nazis wanted to transform the Poles into a caste of slave laborers who would work on the plantations and farms of these German “pioneers.” But below the Poles were Jews. And from the very first moments of the Nazi occupation, Nazis sought to separate Jews from their Polish fellow citizens, to degrade them publicly in every possible way, to violently kick them off of bread lines, to stage humiliating spectacles in the street — cutting off rabbis’ beards, forcing Jewish women to clean the streets with their underwear — and to paint them as disease-ridden parasites upon Poles. One of the things the Nazis did early on, before the ghetto, was stage pogroms. They would get some Polish youth who were poor and drunk and racist, give them some money to go into a Jewish neighborhood and break people’s heads and steal their stuff, get them drunk beforehand, and then follow it with film crews. The reason that they were doing this was that they wanted to stage propaganda films that showed the drunken savage Pole and the subhuman pathetic Jew and showed themselves as the benevolent colonizer who was keeping order — and who everyone was very lucky to have. The Germans really looked to the technologies of colonialism when they thought about how to deal with Poland. The Technologies of Colonialism Daniel Denvir You mentioned that the Nazi occupation of Poland, and specifically their establishment and governance of the Jewish ghetto in Warsaw, drew on models made by European colonialism. What sort of lessons did the Nazis take from that? Molly Crabapple At the start of the Nazi invasion, Poles and Jews fought side by side together on the barricades of Warsaw. Within about a year, they are living in separate segregated spheres, and this is even before the creation of the Warsaw Ghetto. The Judenrat is another idea the Germans took from old-school colonialism: having a local mediating body that would carry out your dictates, drawn from the community of the people you had colonized and were ruling. The Judenrat originally started as local Jewish community workers, businessmen, respectable men whom the Germans told were responsible for organizing hospitals and food. But very quickly, it became a tool of the German occupation, where the Judenrat would be responsible for rounding up Jews for forced labor and eventually, within a few years, responsible for deciding which Jews went onto boxcars — until all Jews went onto boxcars. The Bund was forced to give a member to the Judenrat, as were all of the sort of prominent Jewish factions, and the member it chose was a councilman from Łódź named Artur Zygielbojm. When the Germans told the Judenrat that they would be organizing a ghetto, Artur Zygielbojm urged resistance. He spoke in front of a crowd of ten thousand people, telling them to fight going into the ghetto with their bare hands if necessary. You can imagine the impossible courage of this man. He was smuggled out of the country with the help of the Polish Socialist Party. But the Germans did create the ghetto, and the Jews were forced inside. With that — even though the ghetto would never truly separate Jewish Warsaw from Aryan Warsaw — it was the beginning of the completely separate lives of the two peoples. I want to read you something the Polish Socialist Party wrote about the ghetto, because I think that the Bund’s faith in human solidarity was not wholly one-sided. It was not something that they were dreaming of out of nowhere. It was something that was nourished by actual acts of solidarity by their comrades. This is what the Polish Socialist Party wrote in their underground newspaper: “The burden of all wars and subjugation forever falls on the working man, regardless of nationality. How degradingly cynical is the fact that the walls of the ghetto being raised by Polish and Jewish laborers are meant to become a barrier between them, as if different fates awaited them.” I think that quote also reflects the Bund’s view of what was going to happen. It obviously knew that Jews were being victimized more than Poles, but it also knew that Poles were being victimized in the most savage and horrific ways, that Poles were also having their entire intellectual class murdered. Polish women were being used for medical experiments. Poles were being shot and tortured and enslaved and sent off to labor camps and sent off to work as slaves on farms. So the Bund was like, “We are all suffering under the boot of this occupier.” Inside the ghetto, the Polish Socialist Party did continue to give solidarity to the Bund. They smuggled themselves into the ghetto. They smuggled Bundists out of the ghetto. They gave people fake papers, hid their kids, smuggled their newspapers all over the country. There was a young Polish socialist woman I found who was sent to Auschwitz for distributing the Bund’s party press; she was caught on a train doing that. For your freedom and ours: We must declare a fight to the death against the indifference growing within us. Before the world finishes off Nazism in battle, we must win a victory of morality. We must oppose brutality with active empathy, the debasement of man with the defense of his dignity, and the madness of racism with the brotherhood of peoples. I stand in the death district and look upon its people, Poles, workers, brothers of the same shared earth. They build this terrible tomb. I know the powers from hell construct these walls, not Polish workers who are also enslaved. However, at the same time as the Bund is writing these heartbreakingly beautiful words, they’re also living in an increasingly horrific reality. Even before the deportations to the death camps, over one hundred thousand people had died in the Warsaw Ghetto — of starvation, of typhus, of being shot at whim by German soldier-tourists who would go in and murder people for fun, of being deported to sadistic labor camps where people were asked to clear swamps with their bare hands. And Jews who tried to escape the ghetto were not met with welcome on the Aryan side of Warsaw. In fact, an entire industry of blackmailers sprang up, who would go around Warsaw looking for someone they could recognize as Jewish, someone they suspected might be Jewish, someone they maybe knew from a previous life. Maybe they just thought the person looked sad, and they were like, “Who would be sad but a Jew?” And they blackmailed these people of every last bit of money they had, and then when those, that person had been sucked dry of all money, turning them in to the Gestapo anyway for a reward. This was a full-scale industry in Warsaw of blackmailing Jews who escaped the ghetto. Polish police would also routinely catch Jews who had snuck out of the ghetto and turn them back in. So at the same time as the Bundists are trying to hold fast to this belief in universalism, they’re also confronted by a Polish society that not only has not gotten over the racism of the prewar years but has also been subjected to constant Nazi propaganda about Jews as evil, Soviet, anti-Polish traitors — and a Polish society that is also under the most immense suffering and starvation itself. As we know, starvation and suffering do not necessarily lead to people joining hands. Often they just lead to people fighting each other to live. One of the fractures that starts happening in the Bund is you have the older Bundists who have these very deep ties with their Polish comrades. They’ve been in jail together; maybe they’ve been lovers; they’ve sometimes even married. But then you have young Bundists who are maybe sixteen years old, and they’ve spent the last two years inside the ghetto. For them, this talk of a brotherhood of solidarity is fanciful. What they see is this walled-off prison where the Jews of Warsaw, and the Jewish youth of Warsaw, are dying before their eyes. That split in life experience was very important for the choices that the adult Bundists and the young Bundists make later. The Argument Over Armed Resistance Daniel Denvir On that note, the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising took place only after a pretty substantial portion of the ghetto had been deported to death camps and liquidated. What were the debates over armed resistance inside the ghetto, within the Bund and between the Bund and other factions, notably including Zionists? Also with their comrades outside the ghetto in the Polish Socialist Party, and with the broader and far more ideologically diverse, often sharply antisemitic, Polish anti-Nazi resistance? Why did it take as long as it did for Jews in the ghetto to fight back? Would it have mattered if they had launched the struggle earlier? Molly Crabapple The first thing about Jews fighting back is that we know in retrospect that the Nazis planned to kill everyone. At the time, the Jews did not know that. The Nazis used every manner of lying, of tricking people, of starving people and then offering them bread and marmalade to get them onto boxcars. They convinced people that they were not all about to be killed; they convinced people that if they were just good workers, that they would survive. Also, you have to remember that in Nazi-occupied Poland, any act of resistance, not just by a Jew but also even by a Pole, was met with massive collective punishment. Early on in the Nazi occupation, a young Jewish gangster killed — I forget if he killed a Polish policeman or a German — but a hundred Jews were shot after that happened. So, because Jews at large did not know that they were all going to be murdered in death camps, because this was something almost unprecedented in human history, and also because any resistance they did led to hundreds of unrelated people being murdered, there was a real fear among most average people of any sort of armed resistance. There were countless instances of very young Jewish resistance members trying to put up posters in various ghettos around Poland, and other Jews saying, “Take that fucking thing down. You’re going to get us all killed.” So I think it’s really important to enter into that psychology, rather than using what someone called — I forget which intellectual coined the phrase — the condescension of hindsight. But the Bund wanted to do armed resistance, and it wanted to do it in coordination with the Poles and the Polish socialists specifically. That was because the only way it saw armed resistance as possibly working was as part of a plan to liberate Poland from the Nazis. The Bundists’ vision of what was going to happen was that they would be part of a grand battle to liberate Warsaw — not just the ghetto, but all of Warsaw. However, they were not able to get weapons from their Polish allies. The Bund was the only group in the ghetto with Polish comrades, and they were not able to get weapons until basically too late. Now, I want to talk a little bit about the Polish Home Army. The Polish Home Army was the largest anti-Nazi resistance force that would ever exist in occupied Europe. It comprised all different Polish political factions, from super racist right-wing ones to super left-wing ones. It had huge buy-in from Polish society and was able to enforce all sorts of dictates over Polish society. It destroyed train tracks. It poisoned Nazis with typhus-infested lice that they dropped into their shirt collars. It murdered collaborators. It published the most popular newspaper in the country, even though having this newspaper could get you sent to a camp. This was a massively powerful and rooted group. The Polish Home Army did not have any Jewish political party in it. The closest it had was something called the Jewish Bureau, which was basically one liberal Polish lawyer who had a Jewish wife, and he was responsible for interfacing with Jews as a whole. The Polish Home Army was extremely aware of the massacres of Jews, and it was mostly sympathetic to Jews under Nazi occupation and routinely did chide people — “Don’t collaborate with the Nazis” — but you get a very real sense that it did not view Poland’s Jewish citizens as part of its responsibility, that it did not think it was as obligated to save Jews as it would have been to save Poles. Also, it had a huge resentment for Jews whom they viewed as welcoming the Soviet invaders of Poland, which indeed many Jews did, preferring them to the Nazis. This was not interrogated in Home Army publications. In addition, the Polish Home Army had a plan, and it was a good plan. Its plan was that it would sabotage and murder Nazis where it could. But what it really would do is build up its strength, its men, and its weapons caches until either the Soviets or the Western Allies were close to Poland, and then it would launch a nationwide uprising. The reason was that it knew, from the bitter experience of trying to defend Warsaw itself during the Nazi siege, that if it tried to do a nationwide uprising and there was no one to relieve it, they would all be murdered. There was no way to do a nationwide uprising in Poland without external help. That’s where the Home Army was coming from. It also frankly didn’t think Jews knew how to fight or would use guns, and it basically thought it was a waste of resources to give weapons to the ghetto. Tirst group that starts seriously talking about armed resistance inside the ghetto is a Zionist youth movement called Dror. I think that there are a few reasons why it’s Dror — not the Communists, not the Bundists, not the older, more mainstream Zionists — but this youth movement that decides an armed resistance within the ghetto is needed. The Communists subordinated themselves completely to the dictates of Moscow, and what Moscow said, after Operation Barbarossa, after Hitler and Stalin broke up their friendship, was that you needed a partisan movement, which meant that you would try to send young people into the forest, preferably young people who had weapons themselves. The Communist movement did not see any real value in trying to do a ghetto uprising. The older Zionist movements were terrified of having an armed resistance in the ghetto for the same reason that almost everyone was terrified of it. They thought it was an act of mass suicide. When armed resistance was first discussed, the General Zionist Ignacy Schipper, a left-wing guy, was adamantly against it. He says, “This is an act of mass suicide. It’ll just get us killed.” Dror has three things that predispose it to being the first movement to realize what’s going on, and to know that this Jewish ghetto armed uprising needs to happen. The first is that Dror is a youth movement. It is not a movement with adult leaders controlling it. The cadre running it in the ghetto, the two leaders, are a pair of lovers, Antek Zuckerman and Zivia Lubetkin, and they’re twenty-five and twenty-six respectively, and that’s about as old as people get in Dror. I really do think that sometimes when you’re faced with something completely unprecedented, experience is a disadvantage. It blinds you. It makes you compare what you’re going through to the past, as opposed to realizing that this is actually new. So, I think young people of all the political factions perceived the Nazi genocide earlier and more accurately than older people did, and I think what Dror had that made it different was that it didn’t have middle-aged leaders who could hold them back. The second thing is that Dror is a Zionist movement, and so it doesn’t have Polish comrades that it’s worried about. It is a movement for Jews. It’s not trying to coordinate with a Polish party or with the Communist Party in the Soviet Union either. The third thing is that Dror was a very disciplined left-wing movement where many Dror activists didn’t live with their families. They lived in what they called kibbutzim in Poland, in collective houses. They had a very disciplined and hierarchical way of living already. A lot of times, what prevented young people from going into the woods and joining the partisans was that it meant that you were abandoning your parents. The family structure was really something that entrapped Jews and that even would convince Jews to go to Treblinka. It was that they didn’t want to abandon their elderly parents or their children. So I think having this movement of young, single people who were not living with their parents in some ways gave them a — I don’t want to say freedom, but it gave them a capacity to contemplate things that would be much harder if the stakes of you doing that are abandoning your elderly mother to die alone. Antek and Zivia, by my reading — I may be wrong, but by my reading — are the first people who really grasp that these massacres happening in eastern Poland, and also the start of Jews being gassed in the back of vans, are not just massacres like the kind that happened between 1918 and 1920, but the start of a genocide that no one is going to be able to escape. When they realize that, they decide that the only possible answer is a united Jewish armed resistance. But in order to do that, they need weapons. So they know that they need the Bund, who are their ideological enemies. And in 1942, the young activists of Dror call a meeting of all of the left-wing parties in the ghetto. This includes regular Zionists, I think it includes Communists, and it includes some representatives of the Bund. They make their pitch. They’re like, “Listen, we’re all going to die. These massacres out east — they’re not isolated. This is not survivable. The Nazis want to murder us all. We need to do an uprising.” They also say, “Listen, the Jewish police” — because the Nazis didn’t have the manpower to do all the ground-level enforcement inside the ghetto, so inside the ghetto, you have young Jewish men who are designated as police officers. Often these are guys from very wealthy families who paid bribes to do this, because being a police officer exempted you from forced labor. But the Jewish police are armed with rubber billy clubs. That’s it. They don’t have guns. They don’t really have weapons. So Antek is like, “Listen, these Jewish police — we can take them. We can take them with sticks and rocks. It’s time to start fighting back.” The two representatives of the Bund at this meeting are Mordechai Orzech, a labor leader from a quite wealthy family, a middle-aged guy, and a teacher named Abrasza Blum. When Mordechai Orzech hears this plea from Antek to do a united resistance, he absolutely rejects it. He says, “We are tied with the Polish working class, and we want to do an armed resistance too. But we want to do it united with the Polish socialist movement.” And then he proceeds to engage in some of the most snotty sectarianism that you will ever read in the long litany of snotty sectarianism done by leftists, where he says, “If we weren’t in the ghetto, we wouldn’t even be sitting at the same table as you, and this whole meeting has been a waste of time.” As you would imagine, Antek Zuckerman is horrified. He’s like, “What is wrong with you?” Most historians, most people reading this, are like, “What is wrong with you?” too. When I read this, I always try to enter the frame that even if people are doing things that are exceedingly stupid and wrong, everyone thinks they’re doing the right and smart thing. So why would Mordechai Orzech think he was doing the right and smart thing? It was because any uprising that was solely inside the ghetto was doomed, and also because the Bund had been part of the world socialist movement for a really long time, and it had fought alongside it, and it viewed these people as their comrades, and it thought that the socialists owed them something too, and it believed in these bonds of comradeship. In the summer of 1942, the Nazis begin what’s called the Great Deportation, where the ghetto is deported block by block to the Treblinka death camp. Ninety percent of the ghetto will have been sent to Treblinka by the autumn of 1942. As soon as the Great Deportation starts, the Bund has a change of heart, and the Bund and the Zionists and the Communists again try to meet and again try to make some sort of united coordinating committee. But by this point, the entire ghetto is just a swarming inferno of Ukrainian kidnapping gangs and gun-toting SS men pulling people off the street and shoving them into boxcars. It’s almost impossible to organize anything inside the ghetto at this point, and every single faction just devotes itself to trying to keep its members and immediate family members alive. What the Bund does do during the Great Deportation is . . . it knows early on that these people are not being sent to work camps. The Nazis don’t tell people they’re being deported to a death camp. They say, “You’re being moved to a work camp out east, and here’s some bread and marmalade if you go into the boxcar.” It reminds me of the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, where starvation was used to make Palestinians in Gaza essentially report for their own murders. That was what the Nazis were doing. They completely starved the ghetto and then promised people food if they went on boxcars that they claimed were going to labor camps. They even got people, when they got to Auschwitz, to write postcards back to their families in the ghetto saying, “It’s great here. You should come on the boxcars. It’s fine,” immediately before they were murdered. But the Bund realized that people were being deported to their deaths. It immediately put out newspapers and bulletins telling people to hide or to fight by whatever means necessary. It also got a member named Zelman Friedrich — he was a blond, blue-eyed, Polish-looking guy. The Polish Socialist Party dressed him up like a railway worker, and he followed the trains to Treblinka, where he found blood-soaked survivors of the death camp. He did a report on what Treblinka was that would become the first major Jewish report on the Holocaust and would be smuggled abroad to Britain and to America by the Polish Home Army courier Jan Karski. But by September, almost all of the ghetto had been liquidated, and the people who remained were largely the young, whom the Nazis thought could work. The Bund’s adult leaders by this time were largely either dead — Mordechai Orzech was arrested by the Gestapo during a mission into the Aryan side of Warsaw — or else in hiding, so they weren’t in a position to tell anyone what to do. This left the Bund’s youth movement largely on its own, and it was the Bund’s youth movement that decided to unite with left-wing Zionists and with Communists to create what was called the Jewish Combat Organization. There was also another Jewish group in the ghetto called the Jewish Military Union, made up of right-wing Zionists, which did not unite with the left-wing groups; in fact, they had shootouts with each other inside the ghetto. So even this unity was not a complete one. The Jewish Combat Organization at the start received five pistols from the Polish Home Army, because the Polish Home Army did not believe that it would use them. The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising took part in two distinct stages. The first was in January 1943, when Nazis invaded the Warsaw Ghetto for another round of roundups. They came at dawn. They caught everyone by surprise, and most of the Jewish Combat Organization’s fighters were away from their weapons caches. In addition to those guns, they also had light bulbs filled with battery acid, guns they got on the black market, and primitive weapons like homemade hand grenades. But the January uprising caught everyone by surprise, and the only group that was near their weapons was the young Zionists around the Hashomer Hatzair movement. These are young leftist Zionists whose leader, Mordechai Anielewicz, had been elected leader of the Jewish Combat Organization. They hid their guns under their clothing, wove themselves into a column of Jews being herded toward the collection point for deportation, and at a signal they began shooting. This completely took the Germans by surprise. They had no idea that Jews could fight back. In the moment it takes them to get their heads together, Mordechai Anielewicz manages to wrestle a gun away from a German and disappear into a bunker in the ghetto. By this time, I should say, people in the ghetto had already started to dig bunkers and hiding places for themselves to escape the labor roundups. So he disappears, but the rest of the people are gunned down, and clashes break out all across the ghetto. There are very few Germans killed that day, and not that many weapons are seized, but the shock of the fact that Jews had fought back with guns changes everything. First, it scares the shit out of the Germans, and they will not come back for a while to do more labor roundups. Second, it impresses the Polish Home Army, because previously the Polish populace had really looked down on Jews for not launching an armed resistance and for “going passively: to their deaths. It’s incredibly cruel, the way this is described in Polish underground papers, and obviously they do not note that the Polish Home Army neglected to give Jews any means to defend themselves. They just chide them; they chastise them for not fighting back with their bare hands. But when Jews do fight back, that changes things, and the Polish Home Army thinks, “These people might be useful to give guns to.” But most important, it changes the psychology inside the ghetto, because for the first time people see what looks like an effective resistance, and the Jewish Combat Organization becomes the kings of the ghetto, the undisputed lords and masters of it.
