The Judenrat by this point has no power. No one is listening to them. They’re listening to these young people with guns. For the next several months, the Jewish Combat Organization prepares in every way it can, and the people of the ghetto start obsessively building bunkers. And these bunkers are not just holes in the ground. People who still have money, who’ve managed to hold onto their jewelry or whatever, chip in. They hire engineers who are inside the ghetto. These bunkers have water hookups; they have power hookups. Some of them have phone lines. They have stores of food. This is an attempt to construct an underground city beneath the ghetto, to weather the apocalypse. They also often have weapons caches, because by this time Stalingrad is happening, and there’s a whole crew of utterly psychologically broken German soldiers returning from Stalingrad, where they have just seen hell at the hands of the Soviets, and they are selling their weapons very cheaply to buy alcohol and hookers. In this time, the civilian population of the ghetto prepares. The young fighters of the Jewish Combat Organization train obsessively. They receive fifty guns from the Polish Home Army; they receive a machine gun; they receive weapons training. Michael Klapholz, my friend Irena’s father, a young Bundist engineer, receives advanced bomb-making training, and he becomes the head bomb-maker of the ghetto and starts up all these bomb-making workshops. Basically, the ghetto prepares itself for what’s going to be the final battle. The young people in the Jewish Combat Organization do not think they will survive. They do not see this as them doing a military blow to liberate Warsaw. They see this as a way for them to die on their own terms. They don’t want to die in a gas chamber. The civilians are trying to survive; that’s why they’re building the bunkers. But the Jewish Combat Organization — they want to die as martyrs. The uprising, the real uprising that people talk about, begins in April. It begins on Passover, because the Nazis liked to do horrible things on Jewish holidays. This time, when the Nazi tanks roll into the ghetto for more roundups, the Jewish guerrillas are waiting for them, because they have lookouts everywhere. As soon as they see those tanks roll in, they shower them in Molotov cocktails, and they start shooting. This again completely takes the Nazis by surprise, and they flee the ghetto. And the young fighters see dead, broken Nazi bodies on the street, and they strip those bodies for weapons. This uprising humiliates the SS- und Polizeiführer of Warsaw, Ferdinand von Sammern-Frankenegg, who was completely humiliated by the fact that there was, again, Jewish resistance under his watch, and he is demoted. He’s replaced by an utterly ruthless motherf-cker named Jürgen Stroop. And Stroop quickly realizes that it’s a bad idea to try to roll his imperial army into this urban enclave that is completely filled with tunnels and passageways and booby traps and land mines, and that he has no idea what it is. It’s never even been mapped. It’s been built up into this almost Lovecraftian warren. He’s like, “We can’t go in there. We can’t go into a tunnel and fight these people. We’ll get killed.” So he says, “What we’re going to do is just burn it all. We’re going to burn everyone alive in it. That’s what we’re going to do.” That’s how the Nazis put down the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. They don’t do it by fighting a battle. They do it with incendiary bombs, with gas, with flamethrowers, and they burn everything. I want to talk a little bit about the Poles and what this means for the other side of the city. Because the Warsaw Ghetto is not like the Treblinka death camp. It’s not somewhere else that people can’t see. The Warsaw Ghetto is in the center of Warsaw. There was a footbridge in the Warsaw Ghetto where Jews would cross over an Aryan market. There was an Aryan tram that went through the ghetto. Everyone knew what was happening in the ghetto. It was right there. It would have been like if it was in Central Park. So when the Warsaw Ghetto starts to burn, what this looks like is a column of hellfire in the center of Warsaw, with the sky a demonic red and ash floating over the entire center of the city. Poles, citizens, soldiers of freedom, amidst the smoke of fires, dust, and blood of the murdered Warsaw Ghetto, we prisoners of the ghetto send you sincere fraternal greetings. We know that with heartfelt pain and tears of sympathy, you are looking on at this war, which for many days we are carrying out with a vicious invader. Know that every threshold of the ghetto has been and continues to be a fortress, that we may perish in the struggle, but never surrender. Like you, we breathe with desire for revenge for all the crimes of our common foe. This battle is being waged for your freedom and ours. How did the Polish city return this solidarity, this outstretched hand? The Polish Home Army had agreed to try to attack the wall during the ghetto uprising, and it did try. Two Polish Home Army teenage soldiers were murdered by the Nazis trying to attack the wall. And it did get guns — albeit fifty, but it did get guns. But it also refused to meet with the Jewish command during the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, and it never truly committed to the uprising. As for the Polish Socialist Party, it had given explosives training. It hid people in their homes. It hid children in their homes at a time when doing that meant death for your entire family. It tried its best to get guns for its comrades. But like the Home Army, it agreed that the rebellion should not spread to the Aryan side of the city. The reason that both of these groups, the Home Army and the Polish Socialist Party, thought the rebellion shouldn’t spread to the Aryan side of the city was that the Americans had not yet landed in Europe, and the Russians were still at Stalingrad. By their reckoning, if the rebellion spread, there would be no one to save the Poles, and the Nazis would just crush it. And it made a brutal calculus that the Jews in the ghetto were doomed, but the Poles outside the ghetto were not. So the Polish Socialist Party watched while its friends were burned alive in the center of Warsaw. It tried to save people; it tried to help people. Outside the ghetto walls was a park, and in that park was a merry-go-round. And as we know, Passover is at the same time as Easter. And while the ghetto burned, Polish people celebrated Easter by whirling around on the merry-go-round outside of the flaming walls. That’s the story of how the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising was crushed. But at the same time, I want to say that the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising was the first urban revolt in occupied Europe by anyone. The young Jews, armed with fifty pistols and homemade land mines, held off the Nazis longer than several countries did. And the ghetto uprising would be an enduring symbol whose significance was spread in poetry and in songs around the charnel house of occupied Poland, and which inspired other uprisings. Some of the young Jewish fighters, including young Bundists like Marek Edelman, were able to escape through the sewers from the flaming shell of the ghetto, and they fought until the end of the war as partisans. But I want to say something else about the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, which is that a year later, the Red Army had defeated the Nazis at Stalingrad and had rolled through Ukraine. It had liberated Auschwitz. It had gone into Poland, and it had gotten all the way to Praga, which is a Warsaw suburb just on the other side of the Vistula River. And when it was there, it released radio broadcasts calling on the Polish population to rebel against the Nazis, and the Home Army did. The Home Army heeded the call, and it launched a giant citywide rebellion in Warsaw. After that rebellion kicked off, the Red Army did not go to Warsaw to save those fighters. It waited on the other side of the river, and it watched. The reason it did that was that Stalin did not like the Polish Home Army, and he was quite happy for it and the Nazis to kill each other off and save him the trouble. So the Red Army watched while the Nazis brought in reinforcements to liquidate the Warsaw city rebellion, and while they burned Warsaw, the Paris of the East, and bulldozed it block by block. Then after Warsaw was destroyed and its entire civilian population was rounded into transit camps, the Red Army rolled in to take the wreckage. “They Have to Refuse” Daniel Denvir What, then, is the significance — historically and morally — of this uprising that was doomed to fail? Molly Crabapple I think the significance of it is that it was the most defiant act of the human spirit possible: people who knew that there was no chance of survival and so demanded to set the terms for their own death. But I think there’s something else about it too. It’s not just about the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising; it’s also about what it meant that the Home Army did not support it, and what it meant that it made that sort of brutal calculus. By the time one is thinking like that, it’s almost become too late. At so many moments, different choices could have been made. The French and the British could have upheld their treaty obligations and fought back against Germany when it decided to invade Poland. That’s one thing. The Polish population at large could have resisted the ghettoization of Jews, as opposed to largely going along with it and sometimes cheering it on. The Polish Home Army could have brutally punished the blackmailing industry from the start, the way that it punished people who snitched out Polish Home Army soldiers. The Polish Home Army could have given Jews in the ghetto guns before 90 percent of them had been murdered. At every single moment, there was a chance for different choices to have been made, even though at each moment those choices became more and more constricted. But for me, the lesson of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising is that people cannot let it get to that, and they have to refuse. They have to refuse to allow their neighbors to be taken, to be thrown in jail and concentration camps, to be shut off from them. When I look at Minneapolis, where so many white American citizens risked their lives to get out into the streets and physically, with their cars and with their bodies, prevent their neighbors from being taken to concentration camps — and two white American citizens were shot in the head doing this — that’s, I think, what is needed. It’s that refusal from the start, before it’s at the point where all you have is young people committing an impossibly valiant act of mass suicide. Suffering Sanctifies No One Daniel Denvir It’s not just millions of individual Jews who were murdered. The Nazis destroyed an ancient Jewish civilization in Europe. They destroyed European Jewish socialism as a place-based social world and political project. In doing so, they remade the fabric of the Jewish people from what was disproportionately, though not exclusively — we’ve talked about all of the various factions in Polish Jewish life — a left-wing revolutionary force into, in the case of those people who moved to Palestine, settler colonialists, people who today in Israel often hold fascist beliefs, ideologies that in many ways echo those of the Nazis. You note in your book that veterans of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising were just a few years later undertaking the ethnic cleansing of Palestinian villages. How do you begin to think through the profound imbrication of the Nazi Holocaust and the Zionist foundation of the State of Israel, and thus also the Nakba upon which it was premised? Then there’s also a third catastrophe, a far less murderous one, that spills out of this sequence, which is the end of the Arab Jewish world, a destruction of a lifeworld for which I don’t even think there’s a particular word. Molly Crabapple In some very profound way, I feel like the Nazis won — in the sense that they ended European Jewish civilization. When I was researching my book, I’m going to places like Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Ukraine, and I’m going to these places like Bialystok. That’s near where my great-grandma was from. This was a 60 percent Jewish place before the war. Lviv was 35 percent Jewish. Jews were not a small minority in these areas. Often they were the majority of these cities, and that’s gone. Not just the people, but even the architecture — the wooden synagogues, a beautiful Jewish architectural art form, just burned en masse. These places had their guts and heart pulled out. While there are efforts, and while there are still Jewish people in Poland, and in Ukraine obviously — Ukraine has a Jewish president; there are actually lots of Jews in Ukraine — there’s still a strong Jewish community in Riga. . . . It’s not the same. It’s not at all the sort of intrinsic part of these societies that it was. It’s not the huge percentage of cities that it once was. Poland had 3.3 million Jews before the war, and I think it has seven thousand Jews now. For me, visiting these places, it was sitting with that loss and devastation, which is something I also felt very strongly when I was in Jaffa and I was seeing all these beautiful Palestinian homes that are now Israeli-owned hotels and restaurants, because the Palestinians of Jaffa were ethnically cleansed and forced to go into boats under mortar fire, forced from their homes. Lifeworlds can be destroyed and not come back. I had some real moments when I was in Eastern Europe sitting with that, and also when I was in Palestine, in places like Lod, where there was a very famous massacre. But the thing that sometimes will anger me is that people will tell me, “How can the Jews, of all people, who have been through a genocide — how can a state that calls itself the Jewish state perpetrate a genocide after Jews have been through a genocide?” The implication is always that having been through a genocide ought to have made you better, that it ought to have made you good and understanding and humanistic and compassionate. But anyone who looks at postcolonial countries knows that is not true. Anyone who looks at places that have suffered under the boot of unrelenting violence and oppression knows that it didn’t turn all the people in those places into saints and prophets. It usually just makes people profoundly f-cked up and often narrowly concerned for their own survival. There’s no story about the Taliban that does not include the brutal Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. There’s no story about ISIS that does not include the murderous American invasion of Iraq. There’s no story about the violence of partition that doesn’t include the violence of the British Empire. We’re able to understand that all of these things are not because of the intrinsic depravity of Iraqis or Afghans or Indians, that they’re refractions of the shattering violence that these societies went through. I think Zionism is very much the same. It is exactly the sort of violent supremacist movement that deeply traumatized people in refugee camps so often adopt, because it promises them dignity through strength. It is no different from any of the other f-cked-up exclusivist supremacist ideologies adopted by shattered people, except insofar as it won. At this point, while there are still Jews living all around the world, the two main Jewish centers of the world are Israel and America. And Jews in America are still to this day largely liberals, whatever f-cked-up beliefs they hold. That’s their orientation. They’re not Trumpy fascists. Jews in Israel, by and large — even though obviously there are valiant, brave people fighting this, I’m not saying there aren’t — by and large, their orientation is fascist. It’s not just a problem of Benjamin Netanyahu. It’s a problem of a deeply supremacist and sick society. It’s obvious that these two communities are headed for a divorce. Because believing in liberal democracy — and I’m not even talking about radicalism, I’m not talking about socialism, I’m not talking about anti-colonialism, I’m just talking about believing in basic liberal values — is incompatible with believing in an ethnostate where KKK-style lynch mobs are rampaging around the West Bank shooting kids in schools. These are not compatible things. And I think there is a fundamental reckoning that is already happening over that, and that is about to become much louder soon. But the Holocaust fundamentally changed European Jews. It’s not just the Holocaust; it’s also the failures of solidarity by other countries. It’s not just that Nazis murdered Jews in the most savage fucking ways and then harvested their fat for soap or harvested their gold teeth to put them in Swiss bank accounts. It’s also that they did this while many powerful countries, including our own, chose not to even do the basic bare minimum of letting in refugees, because they were racist. I think it’s that global failure of solidarity — the failure of solidarity of Europe, the failure of solidarity of America — that leads to this feeling of abandonment so complete that it allows this sort of violent supremacist “I will get mine” ideology to achieve hegemony. This is one of the many reasons solidarity is so important: because if it is not extended fullheartedly and adequately, why wouldn’t the victimized people turn to violent supremacist ideologies? You’ve seen it happen over and over again in history. And the blame for Zionism also has to be laid at the feet of Europe and of America, for their horrific failures. And I think the real thing you can see from this is that all of us have the seeds of the perpetrator and the victim inside of us. There is no group of people that is noble on the basis of their culture, that is noble on the basis of their suffering. Suffering sanctifies no one. Daniel Denvir Thinking of Olufemi Taiwo’s work there. Molly Crabapple Exactly: suffering is not a finishing school. The sooner we realize that — the sooner we stop saying that there are the goodies who are the oppressed of history and the baddies who are the perpetual perpetrators of history, and instead start looking at humans in all of their f-cked-upness and capacity for greatness and violence — the sooner we can have some realistic hope of changing the world. Did the Nazis Settle the Argument? Daniel Denvir Perhaps the most profound contradiction that your book surfaces for me is that while the Bund was clearly morally in the right, it’s the Zionists who can argue, in a sense, that they were historically right about Europe: that there where they lived, in Poland, was, it turned out, not their home; that Jews were surrounded by people who would, in many cases, help the Nazis murder 90 percent of them. How do you untangle this twisted way in which the Nazis settled the debate in the Zionists’ favor? Molly Crabapple There are two things. The fact that the Jews of Poland were murdered and that the Jews of the Yishuv, the Jewish community in Palestine, were not does not come down to anything more than historical contingency. The reason the Jews in Palestine were not all murdered by the Nazis was that it was a British colony, and the British — not the Jews, the British — were able to stop the Nazi General Erwin Rommel at El-Alamein in Egypt. And if the Nazis had been able to take Palestine, which they wanted to, they would have murdered every single Jew there, and there was no plan to prevent that. Perhaps people with the condescension of history would later look at that and think how stupid it was to concentrate an entire community that was the target of genocide so close to Europe, in one little place. To me, it’s contingency, and I don’t believe in making your political and life philosophy based on something so utterly contingent. In terms of whether Poland, Ukraine, and Lithuania were so racist that there was nothing you could have done — that these were just incomprehensibly racist places. . . . and ok, there were good people there, there were comrades; no group is entirely one way or the other. But was the society as a whole so racist that Jews would never be able to make a decent life there? To this, I want to talk a little bit about what happened after the war. After the war, a Soviet-backed dictatorship was installed in Poland, and a nationalist insurgency arose against it, and that nationalist insurgency murdered a thousand Jews in the war’s aftermath, equating Jews with Communists — including an extremely famous incident where dozens of young Jews were burned in a hostel in Kielce, Poland, on false accusations that they were using blood to make matzah. Ninety percent of Polish Jews were murdered, but that meant that about three hundred thousand Polish Jews survived, which was the largest community of survivors in Europe of any country. Within a few years, most of those will have fled the country because of the grinding racism that still remained and the murders — which sometimes were about the conflation of Jews and Communists, but sometimes were just murders of Jews who went back to their house and found that someone else was living in it. It would be extremely hard for me to look at that and say, “Wow, people who left were dumb.” I think it’s amazing that people like Marek Edelman, the great Bundist, did stay. He stayed his entire life; he took part in the Solidarność movement that overthrew the Communist dictatorship. He died in Poland in 2009, and the Bund’s anthem was sung over his coffin. Daniel Denvir And he was not invited to the anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising that the prime minister of Israel at the time attended. Molly Crabapple Yitzhak Rabin. Edelman was not permitted to speak because he was not a Zionist. An honor to his memory. But by the same token, most Bundists fled Poland after the war — most Bundist survivors, including people in my book like Bernard Goldstein, who ended his life in the Bronx. It was that combination of the political repression of living under a Stalinist dictatorship, the constant racist murders, and the horror of living in a place that was essentially a graveyard for the Jewish people of Europe. The thing I want to add to complicate it is that it’s very hard for people to know. There have been many minorities — I think about black Americans — who have been subjected to the most foul and murderous and evil types of violence again and again and again and yet still have fought not to colonize Liberia, but to have decent, dignified, free, liberated, and equal lives in the land where they were born and the land that they helped build. I don’t think anyone could look at them and say that they were naive or that they were wrong or that they were doing anything but engaging in the basic human right and duty to insist that here where you live is your country. And the shame, for me, is on Europe. It’s not on Jews who thought that they could fight to make Europe better. Books About Revolutionaries Who Have Bodies Daniel Denvir I want to ask about how you wrote the book, because this is not an ordinary, let alone academic, history. It’s got incredible narrative verve and detail and heart. It is a political history, but it’s told through these poignant personal stories of so many Bundist figures. What sort of archives informed your research, and how did those archives survive? And how did you convert these incomplete, and sometimes nonexistent or destroyed, archives into these fuller stories? Molly Crabapple First of all, I’m not an academic. I didn’t even go to academic college. I never wrote a term paper. I don’t come from this world, and so I had no desire to put on the drag of an academic and pretend to be something that I’m not. I’m an artist and a writer. I also believe that history is everyone’s birthright, and I know that the vast majority of people do not read academic books. They’re not interested in reading them. They find that the prose style makes their eyes go blank. So, when I was writing this book, I was like, “How can I write this in a way that my tattoo artist friend will read it? How do I write this so my burlesque dancer friend will read it? How do I write this so that people who think history books aren’t for them will read it?” I always thought about that. I was like, how do I make this something that will be worth the while of people who don’t usually read history? There were a few choices that I made. The first was that I would do a character-driven book, because people relate better to the stories of individuals than they do to big theoretical tomes. I’m not saying that big theoretical tomes aren’t important; I’m just saying that they will never have a mass audience. I’m just like, I’m going to do something personality-driven. The second decision I made was that if I was going to embark on this, I would follow the things that interested me. And I hate conferences; I hate leftist meetings. I am a DSA member who avoids them at every moment. I also think that often the real things that happen, the real dynamics, are not the official decisions of the meeting but rather the things that happen behind the scenes. So, I’m like, I’m not going to write this book and make it just a list of sh-t that was decided at conferences, because I don’t think it’s real, and I also don’t think it’s interesting. I was like, what am I interested in? I’m interested in friendship, sex, danger, love, people being ridiculous, betrayal, internationalism. I’m interested in the physical world. I am someone who thinks that so much of the fabric of being in a movement is waiting outside a jail cell to give someone cigarettes after they’re out, or marching in the cold when your feet are really cold and the wet is getting through the soles of your shoes, but you’re holding your friend’s hand. It’s staying up really late to hand-paint banners. It’s a very physical thing to be in a movement. It’s not just a head thing. So, I was very concerned with this book being something that was set in the physical world. My father said it was one of the only books he’d read about revolutionaries where they had bodies. The other thing I will say is that I went into this with a huge sense of inferiority. And because I felt this huge sense of inferiority, I was like, I have to know everything. I cannot just read the Bund archives and the academic books. I have to read what their enemies said. I have to read what the Bolsheviks said. I have to read every book about the history of Poland. I have to know what tangos they were listening to in 1930. I have to know what people would eat for breakfast. I have to know how people dressed. I have to know the type of chair they sat on. I want to know what the Siege of Warsaw looked like. What did peasants do with their cows, and were they selling the milk? They were. I wanted to know everything. So I did an amount of research that was psychopathic and lunatic. I wrote a thousand-page book at first — or a thousand-page mess, I should say, not book — and then cut that thousand-page mess into the 380-page book we have now, excluding many, things. Now, in terms of the research I did, I learned to read Yiddish. I studied for two years at this amazing summer program at the YIVO Institute for Jewish Research. It’s a twenty-hour-a-week, six-week, beat-Yiddish-into-your-donkey-brain type of program. I read all of the Yiddish Bundist canon, like Di Geshikhte fun Bund and Doyres Bundistn . These are big biographical dictionaries, so boring, and the official history, the worst-written official history in all of official histories. I read all these memoirs. I was also very concerned with women, because the Bund had a lot of women in leadership, but for some reason a lot of the women’s memoirs didn’t end up getting translated into English. So, you get the impression that it’s a much more male movement than it is. Even if you read the biographical dictionary, which is filled with women — filled to the brim with women, women who are physicians and fighters and orators and theorists. Also, because I decided this book was going to be character-driven, I largely chose who my main characters would be based on who had good memoirs, because I wanted to have a sense of people’s interiority. It’s very hard to get a sense of someone’s interiority if all they left you is economics texts that they wrote. That’s one of the reasons that Sofia Dubnova — who was a Bundist, a poet, and a sex columnist, and the wife of the Bund’s leader in Poland — one of the reasons I really focus on her is that she wrote an amazing memoir called Bread and Matzah that gave you such a view of what kind of woman she was, what kind of mother, what kind of artist. It was the same with Vladimir Medem, one of the Bund’s theorists. He wrote an amazing memoir, and then his wife wrote a bitchy memoir too that sort of supplements his and fills in some holes in it. Because I wanted to write inside people’s heads, I had to read what they said was inside their heads. I read lots of stuff by Russian writers, like the Nikolai Sukhanov book about the day-to-day of the February Revolution, and Kerensky’s pompous and self-justifying memoirs. I read stuff by Bundists who became Bolsheviks, like Moisei Rafes. I read stuff by Zionists. I read the Zionist press denouncing the Bund. And then I read biographies of Zionists, like Tom Segev’s biography of David Ben-Gurion, A State at Any Cost . That was the book that gave me the anecdote about Ben-Gurion in the synagogue losing an argument and then threatening to shoot the Bundists down like dogs. Segev was the one who surfaced that one, not me. In terms of the archives, a lot of it was looking for stuff about Volkovysk, my great-grandfather’s hometown. Also, there are these things called Yizkor books. These are crucial for anyone doing this type of research. They’re combination oral history and amateur sociology books that were compiled after the Holocaust about pretty much every town in Eastern Europe. They’re amazing, because they’re just people’s memories of this town. Many of the most vivid passages in my book, like the part where there’s a fight on Yom Kippur in front of the synagogue, are from the Yizkor book. I find them to be the richest, most amazing resource. I always tell Jewish people who are trying to do family history that if they know the hometown their family came from — if their family came from a town in Eastern Europe, and they know what it is — look at the Yizkor book. That’s where you want to go. I also looked at a lot of regular press archives. If you ever want to think about the degradation of print media, know that in 1905, the Brooklyn Daily Eagle had a correspondent in Łódź reporting on the revolution on the ground. So many of the most vivid things I got were from the Associated Press wire, or The New York Times , or the Herald Tribune . The part when all of these revolutionaries in Siberia who’ve just been freed by the new government are racing to get home to beat the frost, and one of the guys is still in his leg irons because the blacksmiths are all on strike — that’s from the Associated Press. That was from an interview that guy did with AP, who were trying to get to Siberia to interview these political exiles. I also looked at the black press a lot. The New York Age is an amazing resource, and it’s all digitized. I don’t understand how you have this press archive that’s all digitized, all text-searchable, in English, and it’s not constantly being referred to for what the black press thought of things. It really enriched my history, being able to not just quote the Times , but to quote the Age . What did they think about the pogroms? What did they think about revolution in Russia? I also I tried hard to look at photographic archives. For the Siege of Warsaw, for instance, there was this American photojournalist who was in Warsaw when the Nazi invasion started, and I think he was one of the last foreign journalists to be evacuated, and there’s a photo book of his photos from Warsaw, showing daily life under the siege. There’s a march I talk about that Sofia Dubnova is on in May 1917. She described it in her memoir, but I also looked at other descriptions of the march, and then I found there was silent video footage of the march, which is amazing. Then I would really try to look into the world that people were part of. Because ok, you’re a revolutionary, but you’re also someone who’s listening to music, and going to the movies, and wearing clothing. You’re part of your society. I got really into Polish tango, for instance, because it’s so cool — Polish interwar tango, a lot of which was released on a Jewish-owned record label called Syrena Rekord. I found out that one year the hit song was called “Suicide Tango,” by Mieczysław Fogg. And I was like, “This is so cool.” I was imagining someone listening to “Suicide Tango” on the gramophone during this actual incident where Bernard Goldstein and Polish socialists smash up a Polish nationalist restaurant. I was like, “What would have been playing? Imagine if it was this song,” because it was the year’s hit song. Modernity’s Double Edge Daniel Denvir It’s striking, reading the book, that it was the very same modernity that allowed Bundists and their socialist and communist comrades — and rivals, and enemies — to imagine a world of universal brotherhood, equality, and peace. It was that same modernity that facilitated racist, industrial, fascist mass murder on a scale theretofore unimaginable. If the Bund was premised on an excessively optimistic vision of modernity, have we perhaps now, in the wake of the Holocaust and so many other twentieth-century horrors, reverted to an excessively pessimistic understanding of modernity and of what sort of future might lie ahead? Molly Crabapple I don’t know. When I look at what sort of future might lie ahead, as imagined by our Silicon Valley tech lords, all they’re promising us is dystopia. A healthy skepticism of the idea of universal progress is probably good, because I think buying into the idea that technology and progress are always good is what enables people to be such suckers for the promises of fascist Silicon Valley dweebs. But it is also true that there are things about modernity that are . . . almost every week I think about how lucky I am to be a woman born at this time. I think about how even in my mother’s generation, she couldn’t get a mortgage. In my grandmother’s generation, her husband didn’t let her drive a car. All of these huge things that at every level you just had to overcome if you were a woman. Obviously, I’m fully cognizant of sexism. But by the same token, if I wanted to, I could drive a car, and a man does not have to give me permission. I’m allowed to get a credit card. I’m allowed to travel abroad. I am able to have control over reproduction, even though obviously the government’s desperate to take that away — but nonetheless, it’s still the truth. It’s funny — I have gotten into some arguments about this with some of my radical male friends who have told me, “Nothing is better for women.” And I’m like, “No, it is. Truly.” The Jewish Left in America, Then and Now Daniel Denvir Zooming back to look at this century-plus of US Jewish history, these émigrés and exiles contributed to the foundation of the twentieth-century labor movement, with all of its drama, promise, and failure. But an explicitly socialist — let alone non-Zionist or even anti-Zionist — Jewish left receded very dramatically throughout the latter half of the twentieth century. Many parents and grandparents of today’s younger anti-Zionist socialist Jews became liberal Zionists and loyal liberal Democrats. How would you trace the arc of the Jewish American left from the early twentieth-century Lower East Side to today, and where does the revival of a youthful, socialist, anti-Zionist Jewish American left fit into that arc, and what does it tell us about what might lie ahead? Molly Crabapple There are a few fundamental things that really were blows to the postwar Jewish left. The first is McCarthyism. The Left in America did not merely fizzle; it was brutally crushed. The International Workers Order, which was an amazing, huge Jewish leftist group, a sort of Communist-linked organization, was liquidated by the government. Even some Bundist survivors — I asked their kids, “Why didn’t your parents do anything politically after the war? Your parents were so politically active in Poland.” And in addition to all of the reasons you would imagine, like that they were impoverished and psychologically destroyed refugees learning a new language and a new trade — one reason is that they were afraid of being deported as communists. We cannot overestimate the damage that McCarthyism did to the Jewish left. And when you look at the types of people who were called before the House Un-American Activities Committee, it will not shock you that they’re disproportionately Jewish. Another thing is that America has never been antisemitic in the way that Europe was. This doesn’t mean there wasn’t bigotry. It doesn’t mean there weren’t quotas and racism. But America’s fundamental structural racism is anti-blackness and anti-indigenous racism. And all the other forms of racism are largely dependent on geopolitics, in my opinion, and are malleable. But it’s not a place that is built on hating Jews because of the false accusation that they killed Jesus, the way Catholic Europe was. Because of that, there were so many opportunities: people had the chance to go to college, enter the middle class, move to the suburbs. Most people don’t want to be factory workers, and they don’t want their kids to be factory workers. Being a factory worker is really hard. If they’re a factory worker in a garment sweatshop and they have the chance for their kid to become a college professor, they would rather their kid became a college professor. In general, people would largely prefer to do less backbreaking and higher-paid work rather than extremely low-paid work that also destroys your body. And America gave Jews an opportunity to do that in a way that, by and large, they did not have in Poland. Obviously, Zionism and the hegemony of Zionism, especially after 1967. I think the movie Exodus is responsible for warping so many boomer minds. Also, every immigrant group in America loses its language. The grandchildren and great-grandchildren of Italian immigrants today, by and large, don’t speak Italian. The great-grandchildren of the Irish immigrants of yesteryear, by and large, don’t speak Gaelic. Some do, but by and large they don’t. America is just this machine for stripping people of their language and culture, especially during the years when such a premium was placed on assimilation. Even though the Bund tried very hard to inoculate Yiddish into its children, it was no match for America as an imperial project. By and large, the descendants of the Eastern European Jewish immigrants who were socialists or communists or anarchists, or just plain old sweatshop workers, in 1903 — by and large, their boomer and Gen X descendants became liberal Democrats. Another reason was also Franklin D. Roosevelt and the New Deal and the amazing amount of loyalty they generated. That peeled a lot of people away from the Socialist Party. But in general, the descendants of the Jewish radicals of 1903, by 1970, were probably in the majority middle-class liberal Democrats with jobs in the professions. But we’re also going through a moment where the old liberal-Democrat, secure-a-job-in-the-professions lifestyle is being destroyed — and not just for Jews, for everyone. And while the grandchildren of the Bundist sweatshop workers might have become the Democratic-voting doctors living in the suburbs, their grandchildren are quite likely to be the downwardly mobile adjunct getting paid $12,000 a year and sharing an overpriced apartment with three other people despite the fact that they’re in their thirties. I think the same trajectory that’s leading so many precarious young people to socialism is having the same effect on Jews as on everyone else.

articles.title: M*A*S*H is an Antiwar Masterpiece
articles.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
articles.content: In December of last year, I started watching the television show M*A*S*H , which ran on CBS from 1972 to 1983. As a history nerd with a penchant for old TV shows I quickly became obsessed, watching every single episode in under six months. For those unfamiliar, the show is a comedy-drama following the exploits of the personnel serving at the 4077th Mobile Army Surgical Hospital (M*A*S*H) during the Korean War (1950-1953). Intended as an allegory for the Vietnam War, the show tapped into the intense anti-war and anti-institutional sentiment of broad swaths of the American public of the time. The show is unapologetically anti-war and progressive, unrelenting in its insistence that basic human dignity be upheld in the most horrific circumstances. It is extremely well-written and enjoyable to watch, a true classic of twentieth-century television. M*A*S*H may have premiered over fifty years ago, but it still has much to teach us today. Best Care Anywhere Alan Alda stars as Captain Benjamin Franklin “Hawkeye” Pierce, a gifted young surgeon drafted into the war. He has a penchant for pranks and a consistent distaste for military discipline. Alda’s performance is unmatched, and he is truly a once-in-a-generation comedic talent. His sardonic wit, impeccable comedic timing, and old-school slapstick gags combine to create a masterful performance. At the time of writing, the 90-year-old Alda is still acting and speaking out for progressive causes. He deserves to be recognized as one of the greatest American comedians of the twentieth century, standing alongside the likes of Jim Carrey, Robin Williams, and Steve Martin. There was a significant amount of cast turnover spanning the course of the show’s run. Every time someone left, I was very nervous to find out who their replacement would be, and I wondered whether the new actor could live up to the standards of those departing. I was never disappointed. Hawkeye’s original sidekick, Captain John “Trapper” McIntyre (Wayne Rogers) was a zany, sarcastic prankster. His replacement, Captain B.J. Hunnicut (Mike Farrell) is a grounded family man who often serves as a calming presence and voice of reason. Colonel Henry Blake (McLean Stevenson) was the good-natured, borderline incompetent commanding officer of the outfit in the early run of the show; he was replaced in season four by the firm-but-fair, no-nonsense cavalryman Colonel Sherman Potter (Harry Morgan). The whiny, arrogant, and right-wing Major Frank Burns (Larry Linville) was replaced in season six by the blue-blooded and snobbish but cultured and honorable Major Charles Emerson Winchester III (David Ogden Stiers). Rounding out the main cast are the two other characters who stayed for the entire series: the meek and kind-hearted Catholic chaplain Lieutenant Francis Mulcahey (William Christopher), and the career-driven and tough head nurse Major Margaret “Hot Lips” Houlihan (Loretta Swit). The only character swap that is more ambiguous is the replacement of the boyish and innocent but preternaturally competent company clerk Corporal Walter “Radar” O’Reilly (Gary Burghoff), who left the show in season eight. He was replaced by Corporal Maxwell Q. Klinger (Jamie Farr), the Toledo-born, Lebanese-American cross-dressing soldier who spends much of the war attempting to convince the Army he has gone insane in pursuit of a Section Eight psychiatric discharge. Both characters are quite beloved by fans, and Radar’s departure marked a major turning point for the series. The focus of the show is highly varied. Plots typically involve pranks and hijinx, Army bureaucracy, dealing with North Korean and Chinese POWs and Korean civilians, confronting racism, the psychological and emotional struggles of the staff, attacks by the enemy, interpersonal conflict that blurs the line between comedy and drama, and much more. The show also experiments with its own format, for example by filming an entire episode from the perspective of a wounded G.I. (S7E11), following a casualty in near-real time (S8E11), and depicting a soldier who is lingering as a ghost after succumbing to his injuries (S10E10). M*A*S*H is based on a 1970 film of the same name and the 1968 novel that inspired it. Both works fall outside the scope of this article. The franchise received three spinoff series: Trapper John, M.D. , which is not related to the show at all; W*A*L*T*E*R , the once-aired pilot for a show following Radar; and AfterMASH , which ran for two seasons. I would only recommend the latter to the most die-hard fans. “There’s No Such Thing as an Anti-War Film” In a real sense, this quote from the late French filmmaker François Truffaut is true. Accurately capturing the abject horror of war renders a movie effectively unwatchable as entertainment and impossible to distribute beyond an extremely limited audience. No such project could ever appear on network television. At the same time, M*A*S*H avoids the typical pitfalls of other “anti-war” media that actually serve to glorify armed conflict or advance pro-war messages, such as Steven Spielberg’s Saving Private Ryan or Clint Eastwood’s American Sniper. There are several reasons for this. First, the surgeons in the show are not soldiers in the conventional sense. They are doctors first and foremost. Hawkeye, Trapper, and later Hunnicut only reluctantly submit to military discipline. The show does not depict frontline combat or give the sense that a victory on the battlefield is a victory for the cast. Direct engagement with the enemy is sporadic and never glorified. The show makes it explicitly clear that every advance of blue squares on the map in a general’s office sends countless teenage boys to the hospital in critical condition. The surgeons at the 4077th must perform “meatball surgery” on their shattered bodies in the hope of keeping them alive long enough to get them to a hospital in Seoul or Tokyo. This constant drumbeat of “incoming wounded” keeps the show grounded in its values, and many episodes focus explicitly on the unique stresses endured by wartime medical staff. Second, overt displays of patriotism, love of country, and sympathy with American foreign policy goals for Korea are almost completely absent. The show’s thesis does not seriously entertain counter-arguments as to why war should be seen as a moral good or a regrettable necessity. Characters do express belief in traditional American virtues including justice, fairness, democracy, and equality, but it is rarely tied explicitly to patriotism. It is only foils like Frank Burns who demand loyalty, obedience, and paranoia as they salute the flag. Finally, the more “gung-ho” officers, soldiers, and civilians who visit the 4077th are consistently depicted in a negative light. The doctors are often pitted against officers willing to trade young lives for their own glory, bigots of all stripes, war profiteers, adventure-seeking journalists, anti-communist witch hunters, the officious bureaucracy of the U.S. Army, and more. These figures are often drivers of conflict in the series. They nearly always either learn a lesson, receive some kind of comeuppance, or set up a serious and contemplative moment for the main cast. The show is not intended as an attempt to shock the viewer with the horrific, gory reality of war. Its elements are packaged in a way that is palatable for 1970s TV. Episodes are by no means excessively violent, and they aren’t at all unpleasant to watch. But they do send an unambiguous and consistent message: There is no value in this kind of killing. If any piece of popular media can be considered truly anti-war, M*A*S*H is it. Questions of Taste Most of the humor in the show holds up to modern standards. It is intelligent and well-written, and there are relatively few cases in which a joke is made that I consider to be in poor taste. In one early episode (S2E9), the doctors paint a soldier in partial blackface to teach him a lesson about racism after he requests that he not receive “the wrong kind of blood” (referring to the recent integration of the U.S. Army’s blood supply). The message is intended to be anti-racist, but this plot point couldn’t air today for obvious reasons. Some of the accents of the actors playing Koreans are uncomfortably broad by today’s standards. Many Korean characters’ inability to speak English seems to render them unable to speak at all, though this is likely due to the difficulty of sourcing actors who speak the language fluently at a time when the number of Korean-Americans in the U.S. was much smaller than it is today. There are also a few cases in which a person being kissed against their will is played for laughs, most often Major Houlihan. For these reasons, and likely a few more that I missed, some viewer discretion is advised. By the standards of a fifty-year-old show, however, there isn’t much to cringe at. The portrayal of the cross-dressing Corporal Klinger is particularly noteworthy as an early example of what I would consider positive trans representation in media. Klinger is not transgender in the modern sense. He openly admits that he dresses in women’s clothing only to convince the Army he has gone insane, though his wardrobes are quite involved and he obviously revels in the freedom of expression it affords him. Klinger never changes his name or pronouns, he refuses a Section Eight that would require him to admit to being a “homosexual,” and he returns to a regulation uniform and ceases to angle for a discharge after he replaces Radar as company clerk. The most notable part of the performance is how the majority of the cast treats him with matter-of-fact tolerance, and the characters who scorn him (particularly Major Burns) are portrayed as bigoted and petty. Even from those characters, anti-trans rhetoric doesn’t go to extremes. Other trans people have different opinions on this topic. They believe Klinger plays into a harmful stereotype of the “man in a dress” that has been weaponized by the cisgender majority to delegitimize trans experiences. Given how the show approaches LGBTQ+ issues more broadly, including Hawkeye and Trapper’s acceptance of a closeted gay soldier (S2E22), I am personally inclined to believe the showrunners approached the question of Klinger’s identity as carefully and sensitively as could be expected for the time. That said, readers are encouraged to form their own conclusions. Goodbye, Farewell and Amen The series finale is a two-hour tour de force. Its live broadcast was watched by over 100 million people nationwide, and to this day it remains one of the most-watched scripted television events in history. Directed by Alan Alda, the finale does an excellent job of capturing the heart of the show. The episode is perfectly calibrated in its bittersweetness, and it serves as a powerful, emotionally satisfying, and fitting sendoff. There is one rather disturbing plot point in the episode relating to the ultimate reason for Hawkeye’s hospitalization. It isn’t graphically depicted and is handled with care, but sensitive viewers can choose to skip that section, which takes place from timestamps 38:51 to 41:25. As the ceasefire is announced during the finale, the total number of U.N., communist, and civilian casualties is read out over the base’s loudspeaker system, serving as a memorial for all those killed and permanently scarred by the Korean War. Klinger’s question: “Vietnam? Where’s that?” is particularly poignant as a nod to the show’s origin as a critique of the Vietnam War. * * * M*A*S*H is solidly progressive in a way that socialist viewers will immediately recognize. None of the characters are socialists, nor could they be in a show set during the early Cold War. But we can still admire and praise the virtues the show promotes: Radical tolerance of those different from us. Scorn for the horror of war and cruelty in every form. Sacrifice for those who have nothing. M*A*S*H reminds us that we should not apologize for our values, that our most basic humanity must be upheld against the forces of imperialism, militarism, and hatred. The doctors of the 4077th are unable to stop the unbelievable carnage around them. They can only do their best to help those who come through the door. In our own time of global crisis, we should strive to do the same. M*A*S*H is currently available to stream in its entirety on Hulu. articles.title: The Call for Working-Class Liberalism Is Coming From Inside the House
articles.author: Gerard Di Trolio
articles.content: The socialist left has a vexed relationship with major economists. This is a problem, because it sometimes leaves the Left on the outside of contemporary economic debates. Daron Acemoglu is precisely the sort of economist that the Left should not ignore. Alongside his frequent collaborators Simon Johnson and James A. Robinson, he is a 2024 Nobel laureate in economics. He is also among the world’s most cited economists. His new book, What Happened to Liberal Democracy? , has already received lot of attention, as his recent spat with The Economist shows. Acemoglu’s work can be summed up in the proposition that institutions matter for economic growth. He identifies two types of institutions. Inclusive political and economic institutions constrain power, protect rights, and broaden access to opportunity, encouraging investment and innovation. Extractive institutions concentrate wealth and authority in a few hands, shutting out most people from political and economic participation. Extractive institutions may generate growth in the short term, but tend to undermine long-term prosperity. In What Happened to Liberal Democracy? , Acemoglu argues that technological innovation does not automatically produce shared prosperity. Who benefits depends on who controls technology, and how political and economic institutions distribute its gains. This perspective is unlikely to elicit many objections from Jacobin readers. Indeed, the Left’s interest in institutions long predates Acemoglu and Johnson’s intervention. From Nicos Poulantzas and the Analytical Marxists to more recent work by Stephen Maher and Scott Aquanno, Marxists have developed considered accounts of how institutions both reflect and shape struggles among classes and social forces. But Acemoglu’s new book is a useful reminder that these questions remain central, and its argument deserves engagement from the Left. Clearly, the idea that institutions matter is not controversial. But what deserves closer scrutiny is the question of how institutions are made, whose power they entrench, and whether they can be remade. Acemoglu is not without his critics beyond the classical liberals at The Economist . Adam Tooze has argued that Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson have a Whiggish approach to history that puts liberal democracy at the center. Economists like Mushtaq Khan have challenged them on placing such a high premium on the importance of Western-style property rights to set the stage for economic growth. The greatest challenge to this framework is the specter of China. Acemoglu’s account of inclusive and extractive institutions can explain underdevelopment caused by colonial institutions in Africa and Latin America . It has a much harder time explaining China’s rise. Authoritarian institutions may help explain China’s phase of export-led industrialization, like they did South Korea and Taiwan in the 1970s. But it seems less able to explain how the country now pushes the technological frontier in a number of industries. Acemoglu associates high-tech innovation with inclusive institutions that allow for entrepreneurialism, entry of new firms, open debate and research, and patents that protect innovators from confiscation. Not Your Dad’s Bourgeois Institutions The Left has an uneven history when it comes to institutional theory. Some Marxists have, for the most part, treated institutions as instruments of bourgeois rule, drawing on the The Communist Manifesto ’s characterization of the state as a “committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie.” This has encouraged a structural functionalism in which institutions are understood primarily to stabilize and help reproduce capitalism. In fairness, several Marxist theorists have pushed beyond this view. Poulantzas argued that the state was the “material condensation” of the balance of class forces in his 1978 book, State, Power, Socialism , while the Analytical Marxists pursued lines of inquiry that were unabashedly outside Marxist orthodoxy, particularly in their treatment of institutional questions. More recently, Stephen Maher and Scott M. Aquanno have theorized what they call Institutional Marxism (IM). Informed by the work of Leo Panitch and Sam Gindin, the IM perspective argues that state, business, and working-class institutions are shaped by the struggles among social forces and, in turn, give each period of capitalism its distinctive form. This lineage has included some heavy-hitting interventions. Famed development economist and September Group member Pranab Bardhan’s analysis shows how states can tolerate inefficient economic institutions when particular elite fractions capture them, while Vivek Chibber emphasizes that industrial policy cannot succeed without proper design. In this context, What Happened to Liberal Democracy? makes a number of arguments that the Left will nod its head along with and others it will vigorously dispute. The Left will agree that, in many liberal democratic countries, the working class has been left behind, social bonds have frayed, and artificial intelligence (AI), if handled poorly, is a threat to rebuilding a prosperous society. More controversial is his call for a “working-class liberalism” and the political project it entails. Acemoglu starts off by laying out what he believes constitute the great successes of liberal democracies. This is where the Whiggish tendency Tooze identifies becomes glaring. Acemoglu genuinely believes in the promise of liberal democracy, especially compared with its actually existing alternatives. However, it would be unfair to call his account purely Whiggish. Acemoglu frames liberal democracy as an incomplete but essentially progressive project, the failures of which can be cured by recuperating its fundamental commitments. He acknowledges liberalism’s historical failures, such as colonialism and lack of rights for women, but also believes that its successes have contributed to its present malaise. For Acemoglu, this malaise includes the de-linking of wages from productivity. He places greater blame for this on technology than on the declining power of organized labor. He also underscores the growing cultural and educational divide between the working class and what might, though he does not use the term, be called the professional-managerial class (PMC). Culture War in the Digital Age Acemoglu believes that educated liberals’ efforts at social engineering across a range of cultural issues have exacerbated this divide and have led to a working-class backlash. Algorithms and AI aggravate these problems. A staunch defender of free speech, Acemoglu puts forward a novel proposal — regulate the algorithms, not the speech. This would mean social media feeds would show users content from the accounts they follow rather than shepherding them toward the latest outrage or viral post. On the AI front, Acemoglu is adamant about creating what he calls “ pro-worker AI .” Pro-worker AI would help workers perform existing tasks more effectively, acquire new capabilities, and take on entirely new tasks. Any given job is a collection of tasks. AI can either automate many of those tasks or enhance the productivity of the humans that perform them. Acemoglu believes that the current business model and ideological orientation of AI companies give them no incentives to develop pro-worker AI. For him, the future direction of AI is therefore a test of liberal democracy. Responding to AI will require not only state regulation but also public deliberation in the best liberal-democratic tradition. Acemoglu rightly grasps that AI is not going anywhere. Donald Trump could throw Sam Altman and Dario Amodei in prison tomorrow and dissolve their companies, and AI would still persist, if perhaps at a slower pace. The rest of Acemoglu’s vision for working-class liberalism seeks to reconnect liberal democracy with workers’ material interests, social prestige, and political power, especially for those without university degrees. He makes it clear that he values traditional liberal principles of pluralism, freedom of expression, the rule of law, and democratic self-government. But he wants liberalism to prioritize good jobs, rising wages, public services, worker voice, and broadly shared technological progress. Such an agenda would not be out of place at a rally hosted by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Bernie Sanders. A more fraught matter for the Left is Acemoglu’s view that working-class liberalism should empower local communities and accommodate diverse values and opinions, within the bounds of basic liberties, rather than imposing cultural change from above. It raises the contentious question of the extent to which the consent and solidarity of the broader working-class majority can be secured when the terms of cultural politics are shaped without broad democratic participation. The Limits of Working-Class Liberalism Acemoglu insists that skepticism toward social engineering from above must not mean compromising minorities’ civil rights. He points to the example of Ireland’s citizens assemblies , which helped clear the way for the referenda legalizing same-sex marriage and repealing the constitutional ban on abortion, as proof that deliberation among the public in a liberal democracy can produce progressive wins. After its early appearance, the idea of citizens’ assemblies largely disappears from the rest of the book. For all of his enthusiasm for returning to liberal democracy’s local deliberative traditions, there is no extended engagement with the idea of citizens’ assemblies or other ways of enriching local democracy, such as participatory budgeting . This is the problem with much of the literature that seeks to defend liberal values. It offers little vision as to how democracy itself might be deepened beyond making sure existing political institutions start working properly again. Local deliberation is necessary, but it has its limits given the other issues that Acemoglu wants governments to address. As the Center for Working Class Politics’s Dustin Guastella notes , Acemoglu’s working-class liberalism often overlooks the fact that: To deliver broad based prosperity we need to solve major economic puzzles including trade, finance, labor migration, tech displacement, industrial policy, and public debt. None of these issues can be dealt with at the local level. Local deliberation may determine whether a community accepts an AI data center, but it cannot determine overall AI policy. Nor can it develop trade policy. Those kinds of interventions require a central government. The Institution of War Acemoglu also makes the common mistake of making American liberalism and social democracy interchangeable. He supports both New Deal liberalism and European social democracy. In the United States, organized labor was treated as a special interest within the New Deal coalition, whereas in European social democracies, it was a foundational political force. Failing to distinguish between the two leads to a much weaker understanding as to why the United States is an outlier among advanced economies, with its leaner welfare state and higher inequality. There are other notable omissions. Given the book’s concern with the trajectories of liberalism and social democracy, as well as challenges facing liberal democracies, its exclusion of Adam Przeworski is surprising. Przeworski has argued that there is not systemic collapse of democracy around the world, only political frictions resulting from localized institutional instability. Another surprising absence is mention of Amartya Sen. Sen’s capability approach overlaps with Acemoglu’s working-class liberalism in terms of concern with improving workers’ capabilities and promoting bottom-up democratic deliberation to better understand what communities need. The most conspicuous absence, however, is foreign policy. If liberal democracy is under threat in the United States from Donald Trump and declining faith in institutions, these developments cannot be separated from foreign policy. While the Great Recession is often tied to much of America’s current malaise, 9/11, the war on terror and the invasion of Iraq have also shaped our current moment. Spencer Ackerman has persuasively written about how those events led to Trump’s presidency. The lies that led to Iraq and the twenty-year occupation of Afghanistan were bound to corrode faith in government trust. Trump’s dovish act was always a fraud, but it played a major role in his electoral success. The Missing Agent of Change In the 2020s, American democracy is once again threatened by its foreign policy, this time over the genocide in Gaza. Freedom of speech and the right to protest have come under increasing strain . In the same way that the war on terror generated a broader malaise and skepticism toward institutions that contributed to the current situation, the suppression of free speech about the Gaza genocide — and successive Democratic and Republican administrations readiness to allow Israel to act with impunity — will further weaken American democracy over the long term. Foreign policy is by far the book’s largest omission. A further problem is that the book fails to map out exactly how working-class liberalism will come about. When discussing changing mores in society, Acemoglu points to things like civil rights, women entering the workforce, and gay marriage. Yet he offers little analysis of how social movements undergirded these advances. Although the book is a political manifesto, it is hard to understand if it is aimed at building a movement for working-class liberalism or a plea to liberal elites to do better. One of Acemoglu’s most curious statements comes not from the book but from an interview he gave while promoting it. In an interview posted on Bardhan’s Substack, Acemoglu states: I believe that the cause of labor has been significantly damaged by communist and ideological unions, because they have stuck to the ultimately self-destructive policy of working for international aims rather than for the betterment of their members, and in the process they have alienated management. So, in my mind we need a new kind of business unionism. There is a lot to unpack here. Communist-run unions in liberal democracies certainly hurt themselves by following Moscow’s zigzags, though state repression also played a role in their decline in the United States. At the same time, as Judith Stepan-Norris and Maurice Zeitlin have shown in their seminal Left Out: Reds and America’s Industrial Unions , communist-led unions in the 1930s and ’40s did more for racial and gender equality than other union leaderships and had more democratic union constitutions. These are basic values that everyone expects unions to have today, but they were certainly not universal back then. International commitments, moreover, have always been part of the labor movement, even when they were internally contested. Among these commitments, the labor movement can count support for the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War and for the anti-apartheid movement as well as opposition to US intervention in Central America. Today unions are taking a critical stand toward Israel. Acemoglu invokes the hard-hat-versus-hippie divide during the Vietnam War, but, as Penny Lewis has shown in Hardhats, Hippies, and Hawks , there was significant working-class opposition to the war. Acemoglu’s suspicion of union engagement with these kinds of activities actually undermines one of his key arguments: that the renewal of liberal democracy will require workers to have a voice outside the workplace. Taking Power Seriously Acemoglu identifies the decline of associational life as a major problem for liberal democracy. For working-class people, unions were once a key part of that associational world. Business unionism is a subpar foundation on which to sustain it. Unions have played a major role in democratization, notably in Brazil, South Africa, and South Korea. In an American context, the complacency of business unionism during the postwar settlement left unions unable to organize emerging sectors and vulnerable to Ronald Reagan’s attacks. Unions are bulwarks of democracy in the workplace and society, and they should engage in politics at all levels. Implicit in Acemoglu’s defense of business unionism is a concern about the division between the cultural politics of rank-and-file union members and those of a more ideological leadership. Unions can have a progressive effect on members’ attitudes, including toward cultural issues that Acemoglu might regard as divisive. However, this influence is democratic only when unions ensure space for internal disagreement. In order to not blur the line between associational democracy and top-down social engineering, dissent cannot be stigmatized, and open deliberation is essential. These reservations, however, do not obscure what the Left can take from Acemoglu’s book. His book deserves serious engagement. He identifies several realities that the Left cannot escape from: economic growth remains essential to improving the lot of the working class, at least in the medium term; control of technology is up for grabs; and that many working people feel deeply alienated. As the Left gets serious about building economic and political institutions, understanding the trade-offs in institutional design will be crucial. Acemoglu’s work and the economic role of institutions cannot be ignored.

articles.title: Tech Authoritarian Doomsayers
articles.content: In June 2024 , investor David Sacks hosted a high-dollar fundraiser for then presidential candidate Donald Trump at his Pacific Heights mansion in San Francisco, bringing together the titans of Silicon Valley and venture capitalism to pledge their allegiance — and financial support — to the candidate promising to make their wildest tech-authoritarian dreams come true. The dinner party was orchestrated by then Ohio Sen. J.D. Vance, who served as a point of contact between Sacks and Trump, the former real estate tycoon who had notoriously been less than friendly to Big Tech during his first term. This time, however, Trump reportedly struck a different tone, criticizing Bidenera regulations on the ascendant industries of crypto and artificial intelligence (AI), promising to lift them if elected. Netting a cool $ 12 million for Trump, the event helped kick off the new era of oligarchic tech rule in Washington, D.C., that’s shaping all of our lives as a burgeoning class of billionaire elites tears down the pylons of U.S. democracy while ushering in a counterfeit world of synthetic slop meant to enrich the corporate overlords and, if necessary, bring about societal apocalypse for the rest of humanity. Not long after this fateful gathering, Trump tapped Vance — who counts billionaire tech baron Peter Thiel as his consigliere and patron — to be his vice presidential nominee. Following Trump’s election, Sacks was named as the administration’s ​ “ crypto and AI czar,” in charge of unleashing the industry at full force. Today, whatever guardrails had previously been placed on Big Tech have been effectively removed, and the CEOs that infamously sat behind Trump during his inauguration last year are now in full control of our economy — and increasingly our entire political future. The story of that Trump fundraiser is recounted in Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s illuminating new book End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World , wherein the authors, both revelatory thinkers and writers on the Left, explain how the inciters of our current crises are benefiting from the chaos they’ve wrought while plotting their own escape, whether via the underground or another celestial realm. In the book, Klein and Taylor define their subject of ​ “ end times fascism” as: A fascism embedded in an understanding that something immense is ending, and it responds to this discomfiting truth with accelerationist zeal. Rather than alter the human-created economic and social systems driving crisis and collapse, its progenitors insist that it is the human story itself that has hit a wall and that only a small, deserving group of humans will survive the coming cataclysm — whether in their bunkered city in the sky or their bunkered corporate city or their bunkered nation-state, fortressed against alien invaders. … It is a story rooted in that old seductive dream of the chosen few ascending to a gated paradise, while the rest of us are abandoned to the floods and fires of the damned. The purveyors of this dynamic, according to Klein and Taylor, believe that summoning a digital superintelligence through AI justifies abandoning environmental sustainability, so long as they are in turn handed the reins to decision-making power over an unruly public that might have other ideas about how to arrange society. Thiel, for his part, wrote back in 2009 : ​ “ I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” The co-founder of tech giant Palantir — which contracts with the Trump administration to surveil immigrants, supports U.S. military weapons systems and aids the Israeli Defense Forces — is also deeply entrenched with Marc Andreessen, a billionaire venture capitalist with newfound purchase in the White House who believes in fully eliminating the corporate regulatory state and calls himself an ​ “ effective accelerationist” for an AI-driven destiny. These tech authoritarians didn’t come out of nowhere; rather, they’ve been incubating their plans for domination over decades, as journalist Gil Durán recounts in his new book The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. While long perceived simply as governmentally suspicious ​ “ libertarians,” Durán explains that, in fact, the class of Silicon Valley extremists to which Thiel and Andreessen belong aims to take the reins of governmental power to serve their own ends, a process we are seeing play out seemingly every day under the second Trump administration, from Elon Musk’s mass firing of federal workers under the former Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) to the rapid shrinking of government agencies. As Durán writes: Tech fascism bundles powerful technologies — AI, crypto, defense tech, social media platforms, surveillance systems — toward authoritarian goals. These technologies are bound together under the control of a small, interconnected group of oligarchs who, simultaneously integrated into the highest levels of government, are creating an authoritarian infrastructure with boundless power. Its goal, like MAGA’s, is to privatize the public and eliminate democracy. Not content with sporting the full backing of Trump and his allies, this hyper-rich doomsayer set is splurging to make sure their party goes unspoiled after the November midterm elections. The Silicon Valley firm Andreessen Horowitz (yes, co-run by that Marc Andreessen) has already spent more than $ 115 million this cycle — making it the biggest known spender this campaign season. That includes more than $ 10 million to MAGA Inc., Trump’s Super PAC, as well as many millions more to other PACs aiming to curb any oversight of AI or cryptocurrency. Thiel, meanwhile, has poured millions of dollars into defeating a billionaire wealth tax proposal in California, and millions more linked to the tech billionaire are being funneled through dark money expenditures. A completely broken campaign finance system has made this kind of interference in our political system routine. But it also speaks to a deeper reality: the public doesn’t want the future these rich losers are selling, so they’re being forced to burn parts of their fortunes to fend off any democratic control. Far from a gilded status quo pockmarked by data centers and unaffordable groceries, voters are displaying an appetite for getting behind a different vision — one where the working-class majority takes the front seat, and the tech bros and their corporate benefactors step aside. More than 70 % of Americans say that tech companies currently have too much power, and nearly the same level say they support using antitrust laws to go after them. When it comes to overseeing the development of AI, fewer than one in five U.S. residents say they trust Big Tech. Meanwhile, democratic socialists and outspoken progressives keep winning primaries, promising to materially benefit people who work for a living through enhanced social programs funded by stripping wealth away from the real parasites of society — the super rich. From Angie Nixon in Florida, a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member who won the Democratic primary for Senate, to Donavan McKinney in Michigan, a DSA-endorsed candidate who won the primary for a Detroit U.S. House seat, voters are showing a willingness to back campaigns seeking to rearrange society fully in the interests of the working class. The end-time fascists and tech authoritarians want to scare us into believing that a catastrophic dystopia is all that can await us, so it’s best to just go along with their prophetic hypercapitalist scheme. The truth is that we all control our collective future. There’s no better time than now to make that known. _____________________ Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World , Farrar, Straus and Giroux, Sept. 2026 .
